On a Saturday morning in August, Viktor Kruglov, the co-founder and chief executive of the publisher Ranok, was at his headquarters in Kharkiv – the eastern Ukrainian city that, along with Kyiv, is the centre of the country’s publishing and printing industry. Built 15 years ago on the site of a former bread factory, the footprint of the premises is about 10,000 sq metres (107,640ft). Books were stacked 12 metres high on rank after rank of shelves.
Kruglov, along with five senior colleagues, were on the warehouse floor to discuss the approaching school year. The warehouse was holding 628,000 new schoolbooks. “It was the high season of distribution,” he said, “so we were checking all our processes: how to do it more successfully, how to do it in time.”
The meeting was scheduled for 11am. But a couple of moments after it began, there came “the sound of an explosion, and almost simultaneously I saw a huge fire”, said Kruglov. The impact was about 30 metres from where the staff were gathered, and, as colleagues set about trying to put out the flames, “there came a second strike and I understood that there could be a third, and a fourth, so we started to evacuate”.
The munitions used in the attack were jet-powered Shaheds, a recent and insidious escalation of Russian drone technology, faster and harder to intercept than their predecessors. These are the weapons that have been lately terrorising Kyiv during daylight hours, ploughing into the National Academy of Sciences and a working medical clinic in the past week.
“Fifty people were on shift that day,” said Kruglov of the warehouse strike, “and I don’t know how to explain how nobody was injured.”
The combination of an explosion, jet fuel and a warehouse full of paper was catastrophic. None of the books could be salvaged and 8m were destroyed. It took firefighters a week to bring the flames under control.
Several weeks on, smoke still rose from parts of the warehouse. The roof seemed on the verge of collapse, metal beams listing alarmingly, twisted out of shape by the heat.
Shafts of sunlight slanted through the damaged roof, illuminating the catastrophe. The smell was terrible, clinging to clothes and hair. As far as the eye could see, the wreckage of books lay in mounds.
In some places, engulfed by the firefighters’ water, they had dissolved into a thick, stinking, mud-like slurry. In others, they were charred at the edges but recognisable as what they once were: children’s picturebooks illustrated with animals and flowers, geography textbooks, young-adult fiction. Others were nothing but swollen millefeuilles of blackened pages that flaked away to the touch.
A couple of editorial staff, visiting the wreckage for the first time since the attack, looked shaken as they recognised fragments of books they had written or edited. “When you see what was produced with your brain, with your hands, with your imagination, spoiled by Russia, it’s an awful feeling,” said Kruglov, a trim, bald, blue-eyed man in his early 60s.
Those 8m books represented more than 85% of Ranok’s total stock, he said. In the main branch of Ranok’s own Knyholand bookstore in Kyiv, the display still looked cheerful and dense in late September – but, predicted Kruglov, there will be shortages this autumn when the books instore run low and there is nothing to replace them.
In total, this summer, 13m Ukrainian books have been destroyed by Russian missiles or drones – a third, estimates the government, of all books printed in Ukraine this year.
Books, literature, culture and language are not peripheral to Russia’s war on Ukraine – they are bound up in it. The full-scale invasion in February 2022 was prompted, at least in part, by Vladimir Putin’s conviction that Ukraine and Russia have no true separate cultural identity.
Kruglov said he was sure his warehouse full of Ukrainian-language, Ukraine-produced books had been deliberately targeted. “It is nowhere near any military facilities and everyone knows it is a book warehouse,” he said.
Bohdana Laiuk, a Ukrainian deputy minister for culture, who works on literature and publishing, takes a slightly different view: the recent attacks on books should not be seen in isolation, but as part of the invaders’ recent campaign of attacking warehouses, depots and fulfilment centres of any kind. “They cannot occupy Kyiv,” she said. “So they target warehouses around Kyiv to take the possibility of everyday life from us – and books are part of everyday life.”
But books are also part of language, and language is part of identity and, often, nationhood. Books are, said Laiuk, certainly considered important by the Russians invaders. “When the Russians occupy, the first thing they do – and we know this from the areas that were occupied and then liberated in 2022 in the Kherson and Kharkiv regions – is to go to the libraries, take the Ukrainian language books out, and destroy them,” she said.
Until 2022, about 70% of the Ukrainian book market was Russian-language titles – most imported from Russia, some published in Ukraine.
The dominance of Russian publishing had a long history. Its seeds lay in 19th-century decrees under the tsars against publishing in Ukrainian and continued through the Soviets’ promotion of Russian as the language of aspiration, education and culture. Ukrainian writers were purged and Ukrainian literature left in the shadows, shut out from a canon that lionised the Russian novel.
After Ukraine’s independence in 1991, the idea of a commercially successful Ukrainian-language novel that tackled modern social issues was so unthinkable that publishers initially suggested to Oksana Zabuzhko that her 1996 novel Fieldwork in Ukrainian Sex be published in Russian translation. She insisted it was published in the language it was written. It became a bestseller, paving the road for waves of contemporary Ukrainian literature.
Laiuk characterised the dominance of Russian book imports as a kind of colonialism. “It should be compared to how Russians invested in Ukrainian media outlets, Ukrainian TV channels, Ukrainian newspapers and magazines.” It was a conscious policy, she argued. “This is how Russians think: when they arrive on tanks, everything will be ready for them because they already have this information space.”
But in 2022, Ukrainian booksellers abruptly stopped selling Russian imports, in line with the rupture of all commercial ties between the countries. At the same time, swathes of the Ukrainian population switched their day-to-day language from Russian to Ukrainian.
They switched reading matter, too, and Ukraine’s publishers fed the appetite with new editions of classic Ukrainian literature from the 1920s, poetry, translations, and new Ukrainian writing. The country’s publishers may publish Russian-language books, as long as at least half their titles are in Ukrainian; in practice the social barriers to doing so, at the moment, would be prohibitive. (Death and the Penguin author Andrey Kurkov, for example, writes his novels in Russian, but they are published only in Ukrainian translation; he writes nonfiction and children’s books in Ukrainian.)
“People began to understand that the Russians came here to kill people simply because they were Ukrainian,” Laiuk told me in 2023. “So people are asking: what does it actually mean to be Ukrainian? Literary culture gives us the place to understand who we are.”
Oleksiy Erinchak opened the first of his chain of Ukrainian-only bookstores, Sens, in 2021. In 2024, while the city was under fire, he opened a second, in a huge building on Khreshchatyk, Kyiv’s grandest boulevard, to which he has recently added a third floor, with an expansive events space. He has another branch in the western city of Ivano-Frankivsk and he has just opened a fourth, in a former cinema in Lviv.
“When you go to a bookstore like Sens,” said Laiuk, “you feel that you have dignity. You have the right to buy a new book and to choose which one you like. And when you have drones above your head, it gives so much space, inner space in your heart and soul, and in your mind.”
The rapid expansion of Sens is a symptom of something unlikely: a Ukrainian publishing boom amid a full-scale invasion of the country. And now, that boom is threatened by the force and frequency of Russian attacks.
Kateryna and Artem Sova started their imprint in 2023, in the thick of the new Ukrainian publishing boom. By then Artem had been in the army for nearly a year and Kateryna was several months pregnant, living in her hometown of Kremenchuk, on the River Dnipro in central Ukraine. It was their dream: they had both worked in bookstores and at arts festivals for years. Part of the point for Artem was to keep some chink of his old self alive. “I realised,” he said, speaking in Zaporizhzhia during a break from his military duties, “that I was detached from everything I love.”
They began with Lonely City, a nonfiction work about art and the experience of urban isolation, by the British author Olivia Laing. They had loved it since they read it a decade ago, and were bemused it was not already translated. They wrote to Laing’s agent asking whether they could acquire the rights.
“We tried to explain why this book is important for Ukrainians now, and to me personally,” Artem said, recalling. “This experience of being lonely is kind of universal, but it has been multiplied because a lot of people went into the army, and there are so many displaced people in Ukraine: separated couples, destroyed lives.”
Laing, to their surprise, agreed: only then did they actually go through the legal process of setting up the company. articles.title: EU–India Pact Could Expand Bilateral Trade Far More Than EU-Wide Exports, IMF Study Finds - The Policy Edge
articles.summary: EU–India Pact Could Expand Bilateral Trade Far More Than EU-Wide Exports, IMF Study Finds  The Policy Edge
articles.full_text:
Key Details
The October 2026 IMF working paper, EU Trade Diversification Through Regional Trade Agreements, compares the provisions of the EU–India agreement with earlier trade agreements and models their possible effects across 170 industries.
| Measure | Finding | 
|---|---|
| Agreement depth | EU–India covers 36 legally enforceable policy areas, extending beyond tariff reductions. Not all are subject to the agreement’s formal dispute-settlement process. | 
| Bilateral trade | An agreement of comparable depth is associated with an estimated 63% increase in trade between its partners. | 
| EU-wide exports | In a separate simulation, EU–India raises the EU’s total exports to non-EU markets by 0.93%. | 
| EU import diversification | The model estimates an improvement of around 2% as the EU draws imports from a wider range of sources. | 
EU–India free-trade negotiations concluded in January 2026, but the agreement had not entered into force at the time of the paper. The two trade percentages above answer different questions; neither is a forecast of India’s total exports.
The Agreement’s Rules Matter Alongside Its Tariff Cuts
The paper tests whether deeper trade agreements—those covering more policy areas—are associated with greater trade. The EU–India text includes commitments beyond goods tariffs, including provisions concerning investment, capital movement and intellectual property. With 36 legally enforceable areas, it qualifies as relatively deep under the paper’s measure.
Depth is not the same as enforceability through dispute settlement. The study finds that a smaller share of EU–India’s provisions are subject to that process than in the EU–Mercosur agreement. This distinction matters because counting provisions alone cannot show whether every commitment will work in the same way for businesses.
A Large Bilateral Estimate Translates into a Smaller EU-Wide Change
Using historical trade data, the study estimates that an agreement with EU–India’s depth is associated with 63% more bilateral trade. Its separate economy-wide simulation puts the increase in all extra-EU exports at 0.93%. There is no contradiction: India can become a much more important trading partner without transforming the EU’s entire external trade portfolio.
The estimated response also differs by industry. Across deep EU agreements, agriculture, beverages, food and services show particularly strong trade responses; transport and electronics show more modest ones. These are sector-level relationships estimated from past agreements, not India-specific export forecasts. The paper does not calculate a corresponding figure for India’s total exports, GDP or welfare.
India Offers Europe Another Source of Supply
The study’s second finding concerns where the EU buys from, not only how much it trades. Its simulation suggests that EU–India could improve diversification of EU import sources by about 2%, reducing concentration across suppliers. That gives the agreement significance within Europe’s effort to make supply chains less dependent on a narrow group of countries.
The paper does not suggest India is the EU’s largest diversification opportunity in every sector. A possible agreement with members of the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership produces substantially larger modelled gains for green and advanced-technology products. India’s estimated contribution is meaningful, but the opportunities will differ across products.
Policy Relevance
For India, the study identifies a trade opportunity, not a guaranteed export gain. The 63% estimate reflects the historical relationship between agreement depth and bilateral trade; whether Indian firms benefit will depend on the agreement taking effect and on their ability to use its market-access provisions.
It also sharpens the question for trade policy. Sector-level readiness matters more than a single headline estimate:firms need to know which products and services gain practical access, what requirements EU buyers impose, and whether smaller exporters can meet them. Tracking uptake after implementation would show whether the agreement broadens India’s export base as well as Europe’s supplier base.

articles.title: Traders on alert as contagion fears return to Europe's bond market - irishexaminer.com
articles.summary: Traders on alert as contagion fears return to Europe's bond market  irishexaminer.com
articles.full_text:
Traders are on the alert for signs of contagion in Europe’s government bond market after a sell-off triggered memories of the region’s debt crisis 15 years ago.
Up until last week, the bonds of euro-area members had largely retreated in lockstep for much of the year — the result of an energy shock that fuelled inflation fears and forced the bloc’s central bank to hike interest rates. France was the clear underperformer as budget squabbling and a contentious election added to the global headwinds.
On Thursday, something snapped. French bonds tumbled further, along with the likes of Italy, Belgium, and Greece, recording some of their biggest spread moves in years. Germany, however, withstood the pain among big economies as investors piled into the traditional safe haven, a search that also boosted recently weak US Treasuries.
A scenario in which financial stress in one sovereign bond market infects others, even when it looks less warranted, generates the kind of chaotic price moves that worry central bankers, forcing them to step in during severe scenarios. It was a feature of the eurozone’s debt crisis of 2011-2012.
“We are starting to see first signs of contagion,” said Jeff Mueller, co-head of fixed income at Morgan Stanley Investment Management. “If the erratic price action observed on October 1 continues for some time, this may draw some attention from policymakers.”
France has plenty of company in the eurozone when it comes to excessive borrowing, large budget deficits, and fierce political opposition to economic reforms. The heavy debt load of countries such as Italy and Belgium makes them particularly vulnerable in a world of higher interest rates.
To be sure, spreads for the most part still remain relatively low across the continent and the route largely stabilised on Friday, with longer-dated bonds, in particular, recovering. But the pace and extent of the swings have left investors on edge and on the lookout for further signs of disorder.
Ahead of the weekend, market chatter focused on a possible response from the European Central Bank (ECB). One option would be for officials to send a stronger signal that they’ll be more cautious about lifting rates further. Traders have already started paring wagers on further hikes, with swaps pointing to three increases by the end of next year compared with four earlier in the week.
If the signs of contagion intensify, the ECB may consider pausing its quantitative tightening programme, which stops the reinvestment of proceeds from maturing bonds it holds, according to Jamie Searle, rates strategist at Citigroup Inc. That would effectively reduce the supply of bonds that must be absorbed by price-sensitive investors.
Most of the market’s focus has been on the ECB’s Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI), an unlimited bond-buying programme created in 2022 to “counter unwarranted, disorderly market dynamics”. It’s never been used, though its existence is considered a key reason why a full-blown bond crisis is much less likely now compared with 15 years ago.
For France, the TPI would almost certainly be out of reach given its problems are largely self-inflicted. Bank of France governor Emmanuel Moulin has warned his compatriots against expecting a “miracle solution” to come from the ECB. At the same time, it could be deployed if the sell-off starts to look increasingly untethered in other parts of the market.
“If the French election outcome results in contagion to other markets, the ECB may consider supporting them,” said Rohan Khanna, head of European rates strategy at Barclays. “There are no easy choices for the central bank.”
The week’s wild swings were attributed, in part, to the growing footprint of hedge funds in government bond markets. In particular, so-called carry trades, where investors harvest the higher yields available on Italian, Spanish, or French bonds have grown in popularity, particularly on short-dated debt. While those trades can prove profitable when volatility is low, market watchers said the ructions of the past week led to a broad washout of leveraged positions — exacerbating the sell-off.
“Trust me, the ECB is on top of this — they’re talking to market participants all the time, including hedge funds,” said Marion Le Morhedec, global chief investment officer of fixed income at Fidelity International.
“They really want to understand what’s happening and they are ready to do whatever it takes to avoid any big blow-ups.”

articles.full_text:
There’s a common fear among people who work in Silicon Valley: snag one of the fast-growing, high-paying jobs in artificial intelligence, or get trapped in the “permanent underclass”, a phrase describing the fate of those who won’t have upward mobility in the age of AI.
The phrase usually describes a future in which AI automates human jobs. But for women in tech, it’s starting to look like the present.
“A lot of people say: ‘Oh, AI is lowering barriers, it’s equalizing the playing field for women,’” said Urvashi Batra, co-founder and CEO of Prioriwise, an AI platform for IT service providers. “I actually think it’s the opposite.”
Batra said people take her less seriously as the founder of an AI company than her male co-founder. When pitching investors, she and her co-founder have learned that they are more likely to get an investment if he does the pitching.
Women made up only about a quarter of new hires in AI roles in the last year, compared to 50% of new hires in non-AI roles, according to a recent report from LinkedIn. In executive roles, that number drops to just 13%. At the same time, LinkedIn’s research shows that women are more likely to work in roles with high exposure to AI disruption, like customer service, meaning they are also at higher risk for job loss due to AI.
AI jobs, whose postings have doubled since 2023, come with a salary premium, on average paying more than twice as much as roles that don’t involve working with AI, according to LinkedIn’s research. But women who do have jobs in AI are disproportionately concentrated in low-paying roles, like data annotators, said Sarah Steinberg, the head of global public policy partnerships at LinkedIn. Across all AI occupations, men have $45,000 higher median pay than women, partly due to the types of jobs they are likelier to have.
“AI is creating some of the fastest growing, highest paying and most consequential jobs in the global economy,” said Steinberg. “Women are just strikingly underrepresented.”
The ongoing trend could produce the greatest gender pay gap in generations and leave women out of building a technology that shaped the economy, advocates for women in tech said.
“What we’re witnessing is a sort of backsliding,” said Brenda Darden Wilkerson, president of AnitaB.org, a non-profit devoted to advancing women in tech jobs.
Initiatives to promote women in the tech industry have been ongoing for years, with mixed results. Women now hold about one-third of tech jobs in the US. But research has found that women leave the tech industry at a much higher rate than their male counterparts, citing factors like non-inclusive cultures and barriers to advancement.
‘I’ve seen so many women fall through the cracks’
Women working in AI may face even greater challenges. “AI moves extremely fast, and the pressure to keep up is immense,” said Jayeeta Putatunda, an AI engineering lead at investment firm Turing. “I have seen throughout my career so many amazing women I know kind of fall through the cracks.”
Putatunda said it’s not uncommon to be the only female engineer on a team, and that when women are outnumbered, they have to speak up louder to make their ideas known. Mentorship in the AI field, especially by other women, can be hard to come by. And the breakneck pace of AI advancements means anyone working in the field should expect to put in long hours in order to keep up.
“If you have very ambitious career goals in this field, there will be seasons when you work beyond normal hours,” she said, noting that a culture of working 12-hour days to keep up was not uncommon. “I don’t think there is always a neat shortcut around that than to put in the hours.”
Those kinds of work expectations can make it impossible for everyone to stay in the field. “I went on maternity leave for four months, and by the time I came back, there were completely different frameworks and levels of models,” Putatunda said. Getting caught back up was overwhelming. She said it was only possible with the help of supportive co-workers and a husband who equitably split childcare.
“That is one way women get pushed out of AI,” she said. “They don’t lack the interest or ability to keep up. They may lack the infrastructure that makes keeping up possible.”
The AI industry is so new and fast-moving that it should in theory be more meritocratic. No one has a decade of experience working with a model developed one year ago, which should mean everyone has a level playing field. But instead the field has indexed more on personal networks and other loose signals, according to some women who work in AI.
“Companies are hiring at a breakneck speed, but they’re finding people through the same networks, the same referrals, the same filters that they’ve always used,” Wilkerson said. “Generally, that’s not given women the same sort of exposure they should have.”
When people have tried to address these tech industry problems in the past, the solutions have largely come down to giving women more mentorship and implementing diversity programs with goals around representation. But in recent years, companies have aggressively scaled back their diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) programs, largely in response to a political climate that discourages them. That has left fewer companies with institutional programs to hire and promote women.
The political climate has made it more challenging to get AI companies to support initiatives focused on women, said Felicia Newhouse, founder of AI Powered Women, an organization that promotes women’s participation and leadership in AI. Newhouse, a product marketer who has worked in technology companies for two decades, points to the Department of Justice targeting corporations with DEI programs, claiming the initiatives violate anti-discrimination laws. Companies like Accenture, Deloitte, IBM and PayPal have all agreed to pay multimillion-dollar settlements under this enforcement.
“It is getting harder to go into companies being called AI Powered Women,” Newhouse said. “And our advocates inside those companies are also struggling with having women-focused initiatives.”
Still, she said the risk that women are left behind in the AI workforce was something that kept her up at night. “We’re talking about who captures a major new source of economic mobility,” she said. “The deepest risk is that a participation gap becomes a power gap.”

articles.summary: Radulović: Montenegro faces climate, energy and fiscal pressures, Euro model an additional risk  vijesti.me
articles.full_text:

Montenegro is entering a period of increasing climate, energy and fiscal risks, and the new Euro model could further weaken the state's ability to financially bear them, warns Professor Branko Radulović.
He claims that completely abolishing contributions to the Pension and Disability Insurance Fund (PIO) would require at least 860 million euros per year from the budget just for the current level of pensions, at a time when the state already has growing obligations towards healthcare, energy, and climate change adaptation.
"The issue of the Euro model is not just a question of retrograde economic thought, nor just the final act of a disastrous economic practice, nor just fiscal mathematics, which in the short term will cause demand and a certain growth in budget revenues, but also inflation and an increase in product prices, while in the long term it will produce an increasing deficit and growth in public debt, VAT and other taxes and levies, and lead to a reduction or elimination of servicing for certain users. We will become an increasingly uncompetitive investment destination, even in relation to the environment," Radulović said.
The Euro model is a new package of economic measures by the Government of Montenegro, the implementation of which has been announced as of January 2027. It is envisaged that the minimum wage will be 1.000 euros for jobs with primary and lower education, 1.250 euros for secondary vocational education, and 1.400 euros for higher education.
Radulović says that the Euro model is not just a matter of the upcoming parliamentary and local elections, but above all a matter of "the helpless and painful death of Montenegrin citizens, the exodus of those who were vital and intelligent", "cosmic injustice" towards those who were loyal to the system.
He reminds us that the Europe Now 1 program abolished health contributions, which now amount to around 750 euros per capita, at the will of the Government, the average in the EU is over 3.000 euros, and in Luxembourg it is even over 5.000 euros.
"If we expect to have the same medical treatment as Europeans, which is normal, let's accept that this is an impossible mission with this allocation. Even if there is a huge budget deficit, which is to be expected, this much will not be allocated," he warns.
As he adds, the Government has reduced the allocation of contributions to the Pension and Disability Insurance Fund by 50 percent through the Europe Now 2 program, from 20.07 percent to a total of 10 percent. In the first seven months of this year, revenue from contributions amounted to 229 million euros, and the missing funds amounted to 253 million euros and were compensated from general budget revenues.
"According to this calculation, it is expected that the PIO Fund deficit for the current year will amount to around 430 million euros. The Euro Model program abolishes all contributions to the PIO Fund, which means that for the existing pension amounts, if the Government is 'generous', it will be necessary to compensate for an amount of at least 860 million euros."
Radulović therefore asks how the majority of citizens, especially if they are elderly and chronically ill, without any health care or financial resources, left at the "mercy and mercy" of the Government, will survive, especially in the new climate conditions.
Montenegro will be increasingly unfit for survival
Radulović claims that by the middle of this century, and especially by the end of it, Montenegro will be drastically different, increasingly unfit for the survival of existing natural ecosystems and humans, that in increasingly radical climatic and overall conditions it will be unsustainable, and will not even meet the basic living needs of the population for water, food and energy.
"Over time, it will become a geographical concept of a scorched earth, which will be significantly populated by emigrants fleeing hellish climatic conditions, famine or war conflicts. I say this, without false 'blackness', in full mental condition, as a man who is multidisciplinary educated and well-informed. After all, time has confirmed my visions, warnings and solutions many times," he stated.
He recalled a large number of declarations, resolutions and draft laws, as well as algorithms with over 700 optimal harmonized solutions from all areas of transition and key sectors.
"So many open and direct letters and warnings to the leaders. Of all this, only a few initiatives in a modified form were adopted in the Parliament of Montenegro."
The resolution on environmental protection, he added, which he proposed and which was adopted at the end of 2014, set a strategic direction for the country's environmental policy, and it, among other things, established a clear obligation to establish a state Eco-Fund and increase budget allocations for nature conservation.
However, despite the fact that it was extremely analytical and pragmatic, it was not implemented in any segment except for the aforementioned Eco-Fund, which was only established in 2020.
"Nothing about suppressing individual primitivism, cleaning up waterways, technological discipline, remediating ecological black spots and septic tanks, or reducing CO2 emissions, and we have awarded ourselves the title of the first ecological state. Because of some of my projections about the consequences of CO2 emissions and the coming climate hell, I have even been negatively commented on. To make things even more absurd, these 'smart heads' with their purchased diplomas are now 'dealing' with these topics."
Numerous criminal charges in prosecutors' files
He recalls that numerous criminal charges, which he filed against the then highest state officials and persons associated with them "from the criminal milieu" for various criminal offenses, including those against the environment, are still awaiting a reaction from the state prosecutor's office.
"The same thing was done to them, without distinction, by (Ranka) Čarapić and (Vesna) Medenica and (Milivoje) Katnić and (Vladimir) Novović, as well as (Ivica) Stanković and (Milorad) Marković. Despite the enormous amount of evidence, they all remained 'silent' even though it is their duty to defend the truth and public goods."
It recalls the 2020 complaint against the then Prime Minister Duško Marković and others over the contract for the environmental reconstruction of the Pljevlja Thermal Power Plant and the Komarnica HPP project, then the 2011 complaint against the then Prime Ministers of Montenegro and Italy, Milo Đukanović, Silvio Berlusconi and others in connection with the sale of part of the shares of the Electric Power Company of Montenegro (EPCG).
In 2014, he filed a complaint against Đukanović and 31 individuals for alleged irregularities and damage at the Aluminum Plant, and in 2017, against Đukanović, Marković and eight other individuals for the red bauxite case and the ecological devastation of Župa.
"Novović's consistency is extremely disappointing. Namely, after numerous insistences to get an answer about my criminal reports, Novović told me in the Parliament of Montenegro in 2023 that he had issued an order against 16 people. Nothing has happened since then."
Europe is warming the fastest in the world
Radulović estimates that this year's extreme summer is not an exception, but part of accelerated climate change that will bring increasingly longer and more dangerous heat waves, droughts, floods and other consequences for people and ecosystems.
It specifically warns that Europe is warming significantly faster than the global average and that the combination of high temperature and humidity in some parts of the world is already reaching levels dangerous to human life.
As examples of consequences, he cites the large number of deaths during heat waves in France, estimates of possible victims of El Niño, and the massive death toll of livestock in floods in Pakistan.
As he says, the latest report from the World Meteorological Organization on the state of global water resources shows that the water cycle has become increasingly unstable and unpredictable, with reduced river flows and water supplies on land, large losses of glacier mass, and large oscillations between floods and droughts.
According to the Copernicus Climate Change Service, he adds, the global sea surface has reached a new absolute record in temperature and acidity this year.
"Scientists are concerned that the highest sea temperatures are usually recorded in March or April after summer in the Southern Hemisphere, where most of the ocean surface is located, and not in August as this year. The World Meteorological Organization expects El Niño to continue to strengthen over the coming months, so according to previous practice, the next year, 2027, is expected to be a new absolute record since the temperature was measured."
Radulović warns that climate change will particularly affect younger generations, through increasingly frequent fires, floods, droughts, food shortages and mass migrations of people, plant and animal species to colder areas.
It also states that global greenhouse gas emissions have reached record levels, with the largest share coming from energy, transport, agriculture and industry.

articles.summary: Global Factory Activity Gains Momentum as AI Spending Drives Stronger Semiconductor, Capital Equipment and Manufacturing Demand Across Europe and Asia  Spherical Insights
articles.full_text:
Manufacturing activity strengthened across Europe and Asia in September as AI-related investment lifted demand for semiconductors, machinery and other capital goods, although rising energy and input costs remain a challenge.
Global factory activity strengthened in September as improving demand for technology and investment goods supported manufacturing across major economies. The Global Manufacturing PMI reached 53.0, its highest level since February 2022, indicating a broader expansion in industrial production and new orders. A major source of this momentum is rising investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure, which is increasing demand for semiconductors, servers, capital equipment and related industrial products. In Europe, the Eurozone Manufacturing PMI rose to 52.9, its highest level since May 2022, while manufacturing activity also strengthened in South Korea, Taiwan and India. South Korea recorded particularly strong export growth as demand for semiconductor and AI-related products increased. However, higher energy and input costs are creating pressure on manufacturers and raising production expenses. The recovery therefore matters beyond individual industries, as stronger factory output and trade demand could support industrial investment and global supply chains while cost pressures remain a key challenge.
Why Is Global Factory Activity Strengthening?
- AI Infrastructure Investment
AI infrastructure is creating demand across a wider manufacturing chain, from advanced semiconductors and memory chips to servers, networking systems and electrical equipment. S&P Global said stronger goods demand in 2026 has reflected increased spending on AI infrastructure and defence equipment. The expansion is also reaching equipment suppliers as semiconductor manufacturers add production capacity. Taiwan's machinery export orders rose 28.3% to $2.21 billion in August, providing a clear example of stronger demand for manufacturing equipment linked to the technology investment cycle.
- Capital Goods Demand
Investment in machinery and industrial equipment is providing another source of factory demand, particularly in Europe. Eurozone capital-goods output recorded its strongest expansion since the post-COVID recovery, with demand supported by AI and defence-related equipment. Germany also recorded stronger output and new orders among investment-goods producers. This indicates that the manufacturing recovery is extending beyond finished technology products into machinery and equipment used to expand industrial capacity. Such investment can increase orders for engineering, automation, electrical systems and other industrial suppliers across the manufacturing chain.
- Inventory and Supply-Chain Rebuilding
Companies are rebuilding inventories and securing components as concerns over prices, supply disruptions and geopolitical uncertainty encourage manufacturers to strengthen their supply positions. S&P Global reported that inventory building, alongside AI infrastructure and defence spending, supported global goods demand in September. At the same time, supplier delivery times lengthened as raw-material availability and shipping delays created bottlenecks. Inventory rebuilding can therefore provide additional short-term support for factory orders, although its effect may weaken once companies restore stocks to desired levels.
What Do the Latest Global Manufacturing Numbers Show?
- Global: Manufacturing PMI reached 53.0 in September, the highest level since February 2022. Global production recorded its strongest increase since July 2021, while new orders also accelerated.
- Eurozone: Manufacturing PMI rose to 52.9, up from 52.7 in August and the highest since May 2022. Output reached a 55-month high of 53.6, supported by investment-goods demand.
- South Korea: Factory activity reached a four-month high, supported by strong semiconductor and export demand. Export orders grew at their fastest pace in 15.5 years.
- Taiwan: Manufacturing PMI increased to 56.7, reflecting continued strength in semiconductor and AI-related demand.
- India: Manufacturing activity reached a seven-month high, with PMI rising to 55.1 from 52.8 in August as domestic and international demand improved.
- China: Official manufacturing PMI returned to expansion at 50.1, up from 49.8 in August, ending two months of contraction.
- Japan: Manufacturing continued to expand, but PMI slowed to 54.1, a six-month low, showing that the regional recovery remains uneven.
How Is AI Spending Affecting Semiconductor Demand?
AI infrastructure investment is increasing demand for high-performance processors, memory chips, servers, networking components and the equipment used to manufacture advanced semiconductors. The effect is visible in South Korea's latest trade data, where September exports reached a record $120.9 billion, up 83.5% year over year. Semiconductor exports surged 262.8% to $60.3 billion, accounting for about half of total exports, while computer exports jumped 435.3% to $7.0 billion. The figures show how AI infrastructure demand is moving beyond technology companies into semiconductor production, computing hardware and the wider manufacturing supply chain.

Europe’s manufacturing recovery strengthened in September, with the Eurozone Manufacturing PMI rising to 52.9, its highest level since May 2022 and the fastest factory growth in more than four years. The output index reached 53.6, a 55-month high, while new orders increased at their fastest pace since early 2022 and export growth reached a more than four-and-a-half-year high. The recovery was supported by stronger demand for capital goods, particularly machinery and equipment linked to AI infrastructure and defence spending. The Netherlands led the expansion, Germany recorded solid growth, while France, Italy and Spain expanded more modestly.
Which Asian Economies Are Driving Manufacturing Growth?
- South Korea: South Korea is benefiting strongly from semiconductor and automotive demand. AI-related orders are supporting chip production, computing hardware and related industries, while improving factory activity shows that technology demand is translating into wider industrial growth.
- Taiwan: Taiwan’s manufacturing expansion is closely connected to its semiconductor and electronics industries. Strong AI-related demand is supporting production of advanced chips, computing hardware and related components, strengthening the island’s position within the global technology supply chain.
- India: India’s manufacturing sector is gaining momentum from stronger domestic and export demand. The expansion is becoming broader across industrial activity, supported by improving new orders, production and business confidence rather than depending mainly on semiconductor demand.
- China: China’s manufacturing sector has returned to expansion, supported partly by improving technology and AI-related demand. However, the recovery remains uneven as weaker consumer spending, investment and property-sector activity continue to influence overall industrial performance.
- Japan: Japan presents a more mixed manufacturing picture. Export orders remain supported by external technology and industrial demand, but factory momentum has weakened. This suggests that stronger international demand has not translated into equally strong overall manufacturing activity.
What Is Driving Capital Equipment Demand?
AI investment is creating demand across a wider capital-equipment chain, beginning with data centres and extending into power systems, electrical equipment, industrial machinery and factory automation. Expanding computing infrastructure requires transformers, cooling systems, power-management equipment and networking infrastructure, while semiconductor production requires specialised manufacturing equipment. Manufacturers are also investing in automation systems, precision machinery and factory equipment to increase capacity and improve production efficiency. This creates a broader industrial effect in which spending on AI infrastructure supports equipment suppliers beyond chipmakers, linking data-centre construction with machinery production, electrical systems and advanced industrial manufacturing.
Which Industries Are Benefiting From Stronger Factory Demand?

Semiconductor manufacturers continue to benefit from strong AI-related demand for advanced chips and memory. Electronics manufacturers are benefiting from growing demand for computers, servers, networking equipment and other technology hardware. The expansion of AI infrastructure is increasing requirements across the electronics supply chain, while computers and electronics have remained among the key drivers of global manufacturing growth.
3. Industrial Manufacturing
Industrial manufacturing is benefiting as AI and defence investment increases demand for machinery, electrical systems, automation and other production equipment. Diesel prices in the UK have reached a record high, according to the RAC, hitting £2 a litre for the first time as the war in the Middle East continues to drive up the cost of oil worldwide.
The price of a litre in the UK has risen 40.5 per cent since late February, when the US first launched strikes against Iran, while prices are also at a record high in the US, where much of the world’s supply is produced and refined.
In response to rising costs, G7 leaders have agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel within four months.
French President Mr Macron said on Friday that G7 allies would release strategic reserves “up to 100 million barrels, within four months” and “take no measures to restrict the exchange of energy and petroleum products between partner countries”.
Since 2022, the US has become the world’s largest exporter of diesel by a wide margin as the Ukraine conflict has reduced demand for Russian fuel, alongside its ability to refine it.
Around 30 per cent of all cars on the road in the UK are fuelled by diesel, rising to 38 per cent of HGVs. Higher costs to operate these vehicles could have an impact on the cost of goods.
Dr Jonathan Owens, an operations and supply chain expert at the University of Salford, said: “Diesel remains critical to the movement of goods. Heavy goods vehicles, distribution fleets, construction equipment and agricultural machinery all depend heavily upon it.
“Any significant disruption to international diesel supplies can therefore quickly translate into higher transport and operating costs.
“The relationship is straightforward: higher diesel prices increase transport costs, placing pressure on business margins and ultimately consumer prices. In the end, it is likely to be the consumer who pays,” he added.
Why has the price gone up?
The economic consequences of the Trump administration’s decision to launch strikes on Iran in February have rippled across the globe.
The price of crude oil has skyrocket in the subsequent months, from around $60 a barrel at the start of the year to over $100 at several points.
This is a direct impact of Iran’s effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which is the only passage from the Persian Gulf to the open ocean. Around 20 per cent of the world’s gas and oil is shipped through the waterway, with peace talks – so far unsuccessful – centred on Iran’s attacks on tankers in the region.
The cost pressures have had a direct impact on the price of diesel, which is refined from crude oil.
Recent analysis by analysts Kpler found that has largely returned to pre-war levels producers have found alternative methods of exporting fuel out of the Middle East. Around 40 per cent of the region’s crude is now bypassing the Strait, analysis shows, compared with just 17 per cent before the war.
However, the flow of refined products like diesel have not seen the same recovery, Kpler found, with shipments remaining at less than 20 per cent of pre-war levels.
What has Donald Trump said?
In light of rising diesel prices, Trump has said that he may call on European countries to rely on their own reserves as he reportedly plans a 90-day ban on US diesel exports.
Asked about the possibility, the US president told reporters: “We may do that. They have some diesel.”
In an earlier post on social media, US Treasury secretary Scott Bessent, said: “Our European partners should accelerate delivery on their existing commitments and make additional supplies immediately available to address ongoing disruptions.
“American farmers, truckers, and businesses should not be left carrying the burden of a global diesel shortage. America is doing its part. We look to our allies to match their commitments with action.”
Where does Britain’s diesel come from?
Until the invasion of Ukraine, the vast majority of the Britain’s imported diesel came from Russia. Imports from the country have now dropped to zero, with the US and Netherlands taking over as the main suppliers.
Around 31 per cent of Britain’s imported diesel now comes from the US, making up around 17 per cent of its total supply in 2025.
The Netherlands is also the second-largest importer of US diesel, after Mexico. Any blanket export ban made by the US would therefore drive up the price of importing diesel from the Netherlands as well.
The rising cost of diesel is particularly ill-timed for the UK, which has had much higher domestic refinery in the past. From being almost self-sufficient at the start of the decade, Britain now delivers just 55 per cent of its own diesel.
Do we have enough?
Compared to other nations, the UK has a very low level of diesel stock, at just 42 days of imports as of July 2026. This compares to over a year’s worth in Germany (398 days).
Again, this has seen a substantial decrease over the past few decades. The UK had over 140 days of diesel imports stockpiled in 2008, which has steadily decreased as refineries closed. This is save for a peak to over 100 days during Covid, when demand was exceptionally low.
In contrast, the level of diesel in petrol forecourts appears to have remained steady during the conflict, sitting at around 40 to 50 per cent despite the cost pressure. The latest official data only reaches late June, however, meaning the picture may have changed since.
What should we do?
The prevailing advice from the government is not to panic. Transport minister Keir Mather has said that Britain’s supply of diesel was “robust” and “resilient,” adding that the country had a wide range of sources.
Britain joined crisis talks with Brussels on Thursday to discuss whether to release fuel stocks amid rocketing prices.
Delivering advice to businesses, Dr Owens says that “the practical response should be preparation rather than panic.”
“Overreacting or unnecessarily stockpiling fuel and goods risks adding further pressure to supply chains and could ultimately feed through to the public through higher prices or reduced availability.
“The wider issue is therefore one of supply-chain resilience. Businesses need to understand not only their direct diesel consumption but also their indirect exposure through suppliers, logistics providers, and contractors. Emergency stocks can provide valuable breathing space, but they are a short-term intervention rather than a long-term solution.
“For the UK, the message is becoming clear: fuel security is increasingly inseparable from supply-chain security.”

An attack by the copilot on the pilot during a Flydubai flight has raised many questions regarding aviation security, and some of the official versions of the incident have come under scrutiny from online commentators and aviation enthusiasts.
About two and a half hours after Flight FZ1073 departed from Dubai International Airport on Wednesday, it went into a sharp descent before eventually making an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
Media reports said the copilot attacked Captain Smit Machchhar. Passengers were able to overpower the copilot, identified by media as Hamam al-Hammami, after Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door during the attack, which the prosecutor general of the United Arab Emirates said was carried out with the cockpit’s crash axe.
While investigators continue working to establish a motive for the attack, several questions have arisen about the incident more generally across social media.
Here are five questions that are being asked:
Why was al-Hammami allowed to fly despite being flagged over security concerns?
Al-Hammami has been identified as an Omani national, according to media reports.
On Friday, The Wall Street Journal quoted unnamed sources as saying that Omani authorities previously blocked the suspect from flying in the country due to concerns over his ideological views.
On Saturday, CNN reported, quoting a regional diplomatic source, that the copilot had also been removed from flight training over similar concerns and was later reassigned to another position.
It added, quoting two sources familiar with the matter, that the pilot was removed from a job at Oman’s national airline last year over concerns about his views.
It remains unclear how al-Hammami managed to get the Flydubai route despite these security concerns.
The possibility of a plumber stabilising plane before reserve pilots stepped in
Reports have emerged that Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door while covered in blood, allowing passengers to subdue the copilot.
One of those who subdued al-Hammami was Yaniv Hayoun, whom Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu described as a plumber.
In a video with Netanyahu, who met him at the airport, Hayoun, 50, was asked how he knew what to do at the plane’s controls before another pilot took control. He said: “I watch Air Crash Investigation, Mr Prime Minister.”
“I jumped back, grabbed the controls and started pulling back the handles” the way he had seen in the Canadian investigation show, in which experts analyse plane crashes.
People on social media have questioned how a plumber could have handled an aircraft in the air.
No report of mass injuries despite fall of 5,180 metres
According to the flight-tracking website Flightradar24, the Flydubai flight rapidly descended about two and a half hours after takeoff, dropping more than 5,180 metres (17,000ft) in less than two minutes.
While the midair drop caused mass panic among passengers, no one was reportedly harmed, according to the publicly available information about the incident. An Air India flight that dropped 90 metres (300ft) during turbulence in August injured at least 17 passengers.
A flight instructor, who recreated the Flydubai jet’s near-vertical dive in a simulator, said the plane would have exceeded its maximum structural speed and anything unsecured would have flown all over the cabin during the recovery’s negative G-forces.
Why was the copilot allowed to fly despite being an Omani national?
Israel does not have official diplomatic relations with Oman, and Netanyahu has previously said such countries were not generally allowed to operate flights to Israel.
On Friday, Netanyahu said Israel was looking into whether the copilot had acted under anyone’s direction, warning that anyone involved would pay a “heavy price”.
On Saturday, the Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported that government officials had received in advance the list of crew members and passengers who were on the flight, including the Omani copilot.
Security sources told Haaretz that the government bodies responsible for monitoring and checking foreign flight crews landing in Israel are the Ministry of Transport and Road Safety’s Security Department and the security agency Mossad.
Copilot prayed before attack
According to The Times of Israel, Machchhar spoke to Netanyahu on Saturday. He told the prime minister that al-Hammami had asked to pray before the attack. Four or five minutes later, Machchhar was hit with “a big blow” to the back of his head, he said.
The flight departed from the UAE at 7:05am (03:05 GMT). The attack reportedly took place about two and a half hours later (05:35 GMT).
The predawn prayer time in the Emirates on Wednesday was 04:51am (12:51 GMT), which would mean al-Hammami’s prayer did not align with Islamic prayer times.
However, al-Hammami could also have been performing a different personal prayer before the attack.

Temu’s UK sales more than doubled to $171mn last year, as the popular Chinese ecommerce giant exploited a tax loophole that exempts its small parcel imports from customs duty.
The online retailer said in UK filings published this week that its revenues had risen 171 per cent in the year to December 2025, reflecting the growing appeal of its cheap goods made in low-cost regions and sold directly to consumers.
Temu and rivals such as Shein have sold billions of small parcels to shoppers in the UK, marketing products with flashy ads on social media and utilising the duty exemption for parcels worth less than £135.
More than £3bn worth of these customs-exempt packages were shipped from China to the UK in 2024-25, up from £1.3bn the previous year, according to HM Revenue & Customs.
The Treasury said this year that it would close the exemption in 2028, but high street retailers have complained that this meant they would be at a disadvantage for another two years.
In July, the EU brought in a temporary duty of €3 per item bought online below €150 and has promised to fully overhaul its regime for low-value imports from 2028.
Temu earns revenues by providing transaction and online marketing services to third-party merchants, largely in China, giving it a small UK footprint. The company said it had 31 UK employees in 2025 and booked profits of $6mn. In 2024 it had no UK employees, despite booking sales of $63mn and $3mn in profits.
Temu’s UK entity, which says its principal activity is providing “corporate support services to other affiliates”, paid $985,000 in corporation tax last year.
Less than 2 per cent of the corporation tax paid by its parent company PDD Holdings is paid outside China, according to the Fair Tax Foundation, a UK advocacy group. However, Temu has argued that its contribution also includes VAT and other taxes.
“Serious questions need to be asked as to why Temu has such a negligible economic and tax footprint in the UK and across Europe despite its enormous sales,” said Paul Monaghan, chief executive of the Fair Tax Foundation.
“The UK and other European governments need to move much more quickly to not only protect their tax base but allow existing retailers to compete on a level playing field.”
Temu did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title: Own a mobile phone? Then you’re paying the ‘app tax’. It’s a racket and it’s time the UK faced Apple and Google down - The Guardian
articles.summary: Own a mobile phone? Then you’re paying the ‘app tax’. It’s a racket and it’s time the UK faced Apple and Google down  The Guardian
articles.full_text:
Debates around big tech and digital regulation can sometimes feel distant from the everyday concerns of voters. But the power that a small number of global tech companies hold over our lives goes far beyond what most people realise.
As chair of the parliamentary science, innovation and technology committee, I have spent years raising concerns about this: from the data they harvest and the digital “twins” they build of us, to the algorithms that decide what our children see.
But there’s a much less visible example of this imbalance of power sitting in the pocket of almost every smartphone user in Britain: the app tax. Apple and Google control the two app stores through which almost every mobile app in this country reaches its customers, and that position lets them set terms for app developers that most businesses would never accept from a supplier. Sell a subscription, game or piece of software through either app store and both companies now charge a commission of up to 30% on purchases made inside apps, regardless of what the product is or what it costs to make. With no alternative platforms, developers simply have to accept the terms set by Silicon Valley.
Developers are also prevented from telling users that a cheaper option exists elsewhere, known as “steering”. That restriction is enforced by Apple and Google to protect their own profits. For small British developers who might struggle to absorb the cost, that could be the difference between hiring their next engineer or not, investing in a new product or shelving it, or growing their business here or uprooting and building overseas instead.
Consumers pay the price, too. Research commissioned by the Coalition for App Fairness, as reported in the Daily Mail, indicated that British consumers pay approximately £700m per year to Apple and Google, a full £232m more than the companies paid in UK corporation tax last year combined. This is equivalent to around £55 annually for a household with four smartphone users. It is a cost built into the price of the product, invisible on any receipt, that has far more to do with market control and bolstering profits than anything the companies actually did to earn it.
My last job before coming into parliament was with Ofcom, the regulator for communications markets. I was responsible for assessing the competitiveness of markets, because it is through competition that consumers get choice. The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) has found that Apple and Google’s mobile platforms hold an effective duopoly, with at least 90% of UK mobile devices running on their mobile platforms. App developers have no choice but to distribute their product through the Apple App Store or the Google Play Store. If a developer happened to dislike Apple’s terms and another app store existed, they would take their app, and their customers, elsewhere, and the price would fall. But there is no alternative app store on an iPhone, and no practical route for Android users outside Google Play either. Apple and Google set the rules unchallenged.
Parliament anticipated this problem when, in 2024, it passed the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act (DMCCA) with cross-party support, giving the CMA genuine powers to force dominant platforms to change their behaviour. But, so far, the CMA has resorted to weak, voluntary commitments from Apple and Google rather than requirements it is actually obliged to enforce.
Its consultation on “steering”, which would finally let developers point users to cheaper options elsewhere, has now closed and a decision is due soon. Many are rightly nervous that this could end up with another voluntary gesture, rather than a binding rule, deemed acceptable.
But this moment also represents an opportunity. It will be one of the first serious decisions this government makes on big tech, and will likely determine the direction it takes on this issue. The prime minister has been clear, both before and since entering Downing Street, that tech sovereignty means reducing our dependence on a handful of overseas platforms. I want to see that instinct applied to decisions such as this.
This is not about being anti-technology or anti-growth. It is about whether British consumers, British developers and British regulators are able to shape the terms on which technology operates in our own market and influences our society. I urge the CMA to use the powers we gave it, and I urge my colleagues in government to back it in doing so.
- Chi Onwurah is the Labour MP for Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West and chair of the parliamentary science, innovation and technology committee

According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Photolithography Equipment market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The global photolithography equipment market is the foundational enabler of semiconductor manufacturing, directly determining the pace of transistor miniaturization and chip performance. As of 2026, the market is defined by a bifurcated demand structure: leading-edge logic and memory producers are transitioning to extreme ultraviolet (EUV) and preparing for High-NA EUV insertion, while mature-node fabs continue to invest in deep ultraviolet (DUV) and i-line systems to serve automotive, industrial, and consumer applications. This report analyzes the market from 2026 to 2035, providing a data-driven outlook on system shipments, technology mix, regional dynamics, and competitive forces.
The analysis covers steppers, scanners, aligners, and EUV systems, with segmentation by application, wavelength, and value chain position. Key findings indicate that the market will grow at a robust CAGR, supported by secular demand for AI accelerators, advanced packaging, and the proliferation of connected devices. However, supply chain concentration, geopolitical tensions, and high capital costs present notable restraints. The report is designed for equipment manufacturers, component suppliers, foundries, IDMs, and investors seeking a consistent, transparent view of market dynamics and a clear definition of product scope.
The baseline scenario for the photolithography equipment market from 2026 to 2035 anticipates sustained growth, with a CAGR of 8.2%, reaching a market index of 220 by 2035 (2025=100). This outlook is anchored in the semiconductor industry's relentless pursuit of advanced nodes, where lithography accounts for an increasing share of wafer fab equipment spending. The transition to High-NA EUV, expected to enter high-volume manufacturing around 2028-2030, will drive a new wave of capital expenditure, particularly among leading logic and DRAM manufacturers.
Simultaneously, the expansion of mature node capacity, spurred by automotive electrification and industrial automation, will underpin steady demand for ArF immersion, KrF, and i-line systems. The market's value growth will also be supported by the rising complexity of systems, including advanced wafer stages, alignment systems, and control software. Regionally, Asia-Pacific will remain the dominant consumer, led by Taiwan, South Korea, and China, though China's share may be tempered by export controls and domestic substitution efforts. North America and Europe will see growth driven by fab construction incentives and the reshoring of semiconductor production.
The baseline scenario assumes no severe global recession and a stable geopolitical environment, though risks remain skewed to the downside due to trade restrictions and supply chain bottlenecks.

When borders break: Ceuta as a reflection of European migration policy
Ceuta in focus: How a small exclave is challenging the EU
Economic burden of migration: Lessons from the Ceuta crisis
The events in Ceuta are more than just a local migration crisis; they expose fundamental contradictions in European asylum policy. At one of the European Union's external borders, differing levels of prosperity and security collide, highlighting the challenges of border management. While Europe strives for open internal borders and the smooth flow of goods, the control of external borders often remains inadequately organized. This discrepancy leads to the overloading of reception, registration, and return systems during periods of sudden migration. Ceuta vividly demonstrates how quickly a small enclave can become a litmus test for the economic resilience and political credibility of the European Union. The economic and social costs associated with a massive influx of migrants not only strain local infrastructure but also necessitate a reassessment of the European migration strategy. This analysis discusses the key challenges and necessary policy measures that can be derived from the Ceuta crisis to ensure the future viability of Europe's asylum system.
Ceuta as an economic stress test for Europe
When borders fail, freedom of movement becomes a luxury
The events in Ceuta mark far more than a regional migration crisis at an unusual European external border. They expose a structural contradiction that the European Union has managed for years but failed to resolve: Europe desires open internal borders, a large common labor market, and the smoothest possible flow of goods, without consistently organizing the control of its common external border as a European public good. As long as irregular entries remain limited in space and time, this contradiction can be politically masked. However, when a massive influx occurs within a few days, reception, registration, accommodation, security checks, returns, and the sharing of the burden within Europe all come under simultaneous pressure.
Economically, the number of arrivals is not the only decisive factor. Speed, concentration, and institutional responsiveness are crucial. Even a wealthy state can be overwhelmed in the short term if tens of thousands of people arrive at a small border section almost simultaneously. Infrastructure is designed for average loads, not extreme peaks. Reception facilities, medical care, transport capacity, interpreters, security forces, administrative staff, and judges cannot be arbitrarily increased within a few hours. Therefore, marginal costs do not rise proportionally, but rather abruptly.
Ceuta has thus accelerated a debate that was long considered legally and politically untenable in Brussels: Should access to regular asylum procedures be temporarily restricted or replaced by a special crisis procedure in an exceptional situation, possibly orchestrated from the outside? This question is not merely a technical detail. It concerns the economic resilience of the European asylum system, the credibility of state control, and the boundary between legitimate threat prevention and the erosion of individual protection rights.
A sober assessment leads to an uncomfortable perspective. Europe needs a robust emergency mechanism because a system without overload protection remains vulnerable to blackmail. However, a blanket suspension of individual rights to protection would not only be legally risky but also economically short-sighted. It could exacerbate border conflicts, trigger costly legal proceedings, and damage the EU's foreign policy capabilities. Only a viable model that combines rapid control with minimal but effective case-by-case review is feasible.
The exception becomes a systemic risk
Due to its location, Ceuta holds particular strategic importance. The Spanish exclave lies on the African continent but belongs to the legal, economic, and security area of the European Union. Thus, at a very small geographical point, different levels of prosperity, labor markets, and political systems collide directly. A border that elsewhere is spatially separated by the Mediterranean Sea becomes physically visible here and is difficult to control operationally.
The crisis also demonstrated how misleading European averages can be. The number of detected irregular border crossings at the EU's external borders fell by 26 percent to just under 178,000 in 2025. Initial data for the first part of 2026 also indicated a further significant decline. However, the exceptional events in Ceuta were not yet included in these preliminary figures. A single, concentrated movement could therefore overshadow the previously favorable overall picture, both politically and operationally.
This is precisely the key lesson: migration pressure does not behave like a steady, easily predictable demand. It is more akin to a network or liquidity risk. Long periods of relative stability can quickly turn into a peak in pressure. Routes shift as soon as controls are tightened, political signals emerge, or smugglers identify new opportunities. Therefore, declining numbers on a particular route are not proof of permanently reduced pressure, but can only indicate a geographical shift.
For economic policy, this means that border management cannot be based on average annual figures. A contingency plan is needed for rare but consequential events. After all, banks are not regulated solely for normal days, but must maintain capital and liquidity buffers for crises. Applied to migration, this means that mobile registration teams, readily available accommodation, shared transport capacities, interoperable databases, deployable translator pools, accelerated legal review, and clearly defined responsibilities must be in place before the situation escalates.
The economic calculation is clear. Unused reserve capacity incurs ongoing costs. However, a lack of reserve capacity leads to significantly higher costs in a crisis due to improvised accommodation, overtime, security issues, political conflicts, border controls within the Schengen Area, and lengthy procedures. Resilience is therefore not a waste, but rather insurance against institutional failure.
Small exclave, huge cost shock
The scale of the Ceuta crisis only becomes clear when considered in relation to the local economic and demographic structure. Ceuta has approximately 84,000 inhabitants. In 2025, the local unemployment rate was nearly 25 percent, with youth unemployment exceeding 50 percent. The gross domestic product per capita, adjusted for purchasing power, reached only about two-thirds of the EU average. Even without exceptional migration, the exclave is therefore fiscally and socially more vulnerable than prosperous European metropolitan areas.
When more than 70,000 people cross the border within a short period, this is almost equivalent to the entire resident population. No municipal system can cope with such a relative shock on its own. If a comparable ratio were applied to a major German city with one million inhabitants, it would involve a sudden influx of several hundred thousand people. This ratio explains why a state of emergency arises even if a large proportion of those arriving quickly return or are repatriated.
The immediate costs initially relate to accommodation, food, basic medical care, registration, security, and transport. Added to this are costs that are often underestimated in political debates: lost working time for local authorities, displacement of regular administrative tasks, strain on schools and youth services, additional waste disposal, damage to infrastructure, restrictions on trade, and losses in tourism. For unaccompanied minors, the long-term obligations increase particularly sharply because care, guardianship, education, and, if necessary, accommodation must be organized for years.
For Ceuta, reputational damage is also a significant factor. Images of overcrowded facilities or makeshift camps can deter visitors, investors, and skilled workers. In a small, service-oriented regional economy, uncertainty impacts consumption and employment more quickly than in a diversified economy. Local businesses suffer when transport routes are blocked, supply chains disrupted, or border controls tightened.
From an economic perspective, it is therefore wrong to treat the crisis as a purely Spanish matter. Ceuta protects an EU external border, while the benefits of open internal borders accrue to all member states. If the financing is left solely to the border state or even the affected municipality, a classic free-rider problem arises. Other states benefit from the protection without bearing the full costs. European financing of prevention and crisis response is therefore not an act of voluntary solidarity, but rather the appropriate financing of a common good.
Border protection is economic policy
The Schengen Area is one of Europe's most economically valuable integration achievements. Companies can organize supply chains across borders, workers can commute, tourists can travel, and freight forwarders can transport goods without being systematically checked at every internal border. However, this efficiency rests on a tacit assumption: the external border must be controlled in such a way that member states do not permanently reintroduce their own controls for security or migration reasons.
If external borders visibly fail, domestic political incentives for unilateral national action arise. Additional controls at internal borders lengthen transport times, increase fuel consumption, hinder just-in-time production, and tie up personnel in the police, customs, and businesses. Even minor delays can multiply along tightly scheduled supply chains. Logistics, the automotive industry, food retail, tourism, and cross-border services are particularly affected.

Catalan regional president Salvador Illa confirmed the second death in a social media post on Sunday.
Firefighters said the missing person had been swept away by a stream in Pineda de Mar, a town north of Barcelona.
Catalan Civil Protection has sent a new Es-Alert on Sunday to the mobile phones of residents in Vallès Oriental, Maresme, la Selva, Baix Empordà and Gironès.
The message urges people to comply with travel restrictions while the torrential rain continues. Residents in the affected counties are advised to avoid all non-essential journeys.
At 16:48 on Saturday, another Es-Alert was sent to 20 Catalan counties, recommending that all activities and travel be suspended from 20:00. The alert warned that the severe weather could persist until 14:00 on Sunday.
Heavy rain has been falling since midday on Saturday along a stretch of the Catalan coast, which remains under an emergency alert due to the formation of a convective mesoscale system over the Mediterranean.
By midnight on Sunday, between 100 and 200 litres of rain per square metre had fallen across Barcelonès. Meteocat recorded 190.8 litres in the Raval, 170.3 in the University Zone on Diagonal Avenue — the highest total in 18 years — and 152 around the Badalona Museum, (highest figure in 21 years).
In the Raval, 3.4 litres fell in a single minute and 36.1 litres in just half an hour. According to Meteocat, the total was almost double the 95.4 litres recorded in the neighbourhood on 24 March 2017.
The agency said heavy and torrential rain continued into the early hours of Sunday, with bands of showers slowly moving northwards across Catalonia.
"We still have hours to go," Meteocat warned on social media, adding that rainfall totals would be exceptional both in terms of volume and geographical extent.
The president of the Government of Catalonia, Salvador Illa, has urged citizens "not to let their guard down". He spoke of "a complicated night" and an episode that "has not yet come to an end".
Rivers on alert, rescues and trains halted
The Catalan Water Agency (ACA) has reported that the final stretch of the Besòs has exceeded the danger threshold, with an imminent risk of flooding. At 03:00 the river was flowing through Santa Coloma de Gramenet with a discharge of 520 cubic metres per second, and the ACA issued a hydrological risk warning.
By three in the morning, Catalonia's fire service had received 682 calls, most of them about flooding, and had not yet dealt with incidents involving serious injuries. Barcelona's Bombers logged a total of 910 calls and 145 operations related to the storm by 7:20.
At 05:10 firefighters were called to Granollers because of a violent downpour and the sudden swelling of streams. They are working to rescue several people trapped in their cars at the approaches to a flooded roundabout, some of them standing on the roofs of their vehicles.
Heavy rain overnight in Biscay as well
On Saturday the storm also affected northern Spain. The Basque country emergency centre recorded a total of 150 rain-related incidents in the province of Biscay by 20:30, 137 of them in Bilbao, with flooding and pools of water on the roads. In some parts of the Old Town the water reached knee height, and several residents were unable to get into their homes. Some businesses put up wooden boards to keep the water out.
Traffic through the La Avanzada tunnels in Leioa was cut off, and similar incidents were reported in Getxo, Basauri, Laudio, Galdakao, Sestao and Erandio. Euskalmet kept the orange alert in place until 00:00, when the rain was expected to ease, before switching to a yellow advisory until 06:00 on Sunday.

Over 700 jobs are now at risk as a major UK firm has entered administration again, making it the second time this year.
According to records published by The Gazette, NCP Commercial Services Ltd has once again entered administration.
The move follows a difficult period for the parking operator, which has faced ongoing financial pressures linked to changing travel habits and lower demand for car parking since the pandemic.
NCP (National Car Parks) Commercial Services Ltd, founded in London in 1931, manages and operates car parks across the UK.

It offers “a fantastic amount of choice” to customers when it comes to finding somewhere to park their vehicles.
On its website, it says: “We’re passionate about parking services.

The car park operator says it has more than 200,000 car park spaces across more than 800 sites across the UK.
