Edward Williams, Timothy Andrew Higgins and David Robert Baxendale of PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) were appointed as joint administrators on September 30, 2026, according to The Gazette.
The business, owned by Japanese group Park24, had already called in administrators earlier this year, with 682 jobs put at risk in March 2026.

The company said evolving commuting patterns and changes in the way consumers travel had reduced occupancy levels across a number of its sites.

articles.title: France Nears a Debt Crisis That Could Hit the Global Economy - logos-pres.md
articles.summary: France Nears a Debt Crisis That Could Hit the Global Economy  logos-pres.md
articles.full_text:
There is every reason to fear that a French sovereign-debt crisis would have global spillover effects. France is the European Union’s second-largest economy, with a debt many times the size of Greece’s circa 2010. Moreover, France’s debt problems are mounting at a time when bond yields in the United States, Japan, and the United Kingdom have all surged to multi-decade highs.
Not only has France’s public debt ballooned from a little over 80% of GDP in 2010 to 119% today, but budget deficits reaching 5% of GDP continue to add to the problem. Worse, remaining on this unsustainable trajectory has become even costlier now that the French ten-year government bond yield has shot up to 4.81%. With a sclerotic economy that is being buffeted by an energy-price shock and higher interest rates—and which is officially projected to grow by less than 1% next year—France cannot hope to grow its way out of its debt problem.
There is a lack of political will
To date, France has shown little political will to consolidate its budget and cut public spending, which now amounts to a staggering 58% of GDP. Over the past five years, French President Emmanuel Macron’s administration has churned through six prime ministers, not one of whom has managed to reduce the budget deficit in any meaningful way. Deficit-reduction targets have repeatedly been softened, planned spending cuts and pension reforms have been diluted, and promised savings have fallen short of what was initially announced. So polarized is the National Assembly that reaching a consensus on how to achieve debt sustainability remains out of reach.
With a presidential election coming next April, little can be expected in terms of budget consolidation. All the candidates have an incentive to make lofty campaign promises, not to confront the electorate with painful economic-policy choices. Moreover, it is far from clear that any successor to Macron would be able to push through the economic reforms that the situation demands. For that to happen, the next president would need to win a working majority in the National Assembly, elections for which could take place several weeks after the presidential vote.
Even if France had the political will to address its public debt problem, doing so within the euro straitjacket would not be easy. France can neither pursue a currency depreciation nor cut interest rates to offset the contractionary effect of belt-tightening. Putting its fiscal house in order therefore comes with a high chance of recession (especially given the economy’s current weakness); and a recession, in turn, would limit the potential gains from belt-tightening, by requiring increased social spending alongside reduced government revenue.
Markets seem to have taken note of France’s unsustainable public finances and political dysfunction. The spread between French and German long-term interest rates has increased to 119 basis points, its highest level since the 2010 sovereign-debt crisis. The risk now is of a doom loop, where the French government’s rising debt and higher borrowing costs exacerbate each other.
France’s national debt could lead to the break-up of the eurozone
The good news is that the European Central Bank is better equipped than it was in 2010 to support a eurozone member state that is coming under market pressure. Its Transmission Protection Instrument, for example, allows it to buy unlimited quantities of a member’s government bonds in the secondary market, provided that the country has a credible economic-adjustment program in place.
But France would be making a big mistake if it came to rely too much on an ECB safety net. Given the rise of Germany’s right-wing, nationalist Alternative für Deutschland party, there would probably be little to no German public support for another ECB-orchestrated bailout of a fiscally irresponsible neighbor.
Even if France’s mounting debt does not lead to the breakup of the euro, a new crisis for the common currency and tensions between the EU’s two largest economies is the last thing that the world economy and financial markets need right now.
Desmond Lachman,
a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, is a former deputy director of the International Monetary Fund’s Policy Development and Review Department and a former chief emerging-market economic strategist at Salomon Smith Barney.

articles.title: I am obsessed with the ignorance of the Jew-haters - telegraph.co.uk
articles.summary: I am obsessed with the ignorance of the Jew-haters  telegraph.co.uk
articles.full_text:
I need a new hobby to take my mind off my obsession. The catch, of course, if you happen to have an obsessive personality, is that you become obsessed with your new hobby. In my teenage years, on my father’s advice, I played table tennis to take my mind off falling in love with every girl I met. I was quickly obsessed. I lived and would willingly have died for the game.
Even in my dreams I played table tennis, competing against faceless, impregnable opponents. Back the ball came no matter how hard I hit it, until I woke in the early dawn, defeated and exhausted. When I described my condition to my doctor, he advised me to find a new hobby. “What, like falling in love with every girl I meet?” I asked with a twisted laugh. He put a stethoscope to my chest. “That would certainly be more normal,” he said.
The obsession I need a hobby to take my mind off today is Jew-hating. Its omnipresence. Its implacability. Its inexplicable rage, as though it’s the Jew-hater rather than the Jew-hated who has reason to be aggrieved. Above all what obsesses me is the paradox of its uncouth ignorance appealing most to the educated.
Not in the wild or in a zoo do Jew-haters find a home but on the campuses of our best universities, where they might be expected to have read a little history or know the meaning of simple words. Could it be that the ultimate aim of education is anti-Semitism? I serve the question into the darkness, but only a ball comes back, twice as hard as I hit it.
As in my table tennis years, the nights are the worst. The minute my eyes close the Jew haters appear, not marching – my bed is not big enough to accommodate any sort of demonstration – but sitting packed tight in lecture theatres, wearing black armbands and that closed expression favoured by people who never question themselves. “Shalom aleichem,” I begin. Peace be upon you. They don’t chant the customary “Aleichem shalom”, in return.
I begin by filling in the blanks in their knowledge. Tell them Jesus was a Jew and would certainly have been a Zionist had he been alive when the Jews were being killed in their tens of thousands in pogroms throughout eastern Europe. I tell them what a pogrom was.
I explain that Zionism was a movement of liberation and self-realization of the sort they support when it’s for Palestinians. Zionists didn’t turn up out of the blue in tanks firing Kalashnikovs. They came carrying shovels and works of philosophy. Some were idealists and dreamers, poets and utopists, others, no doubt, would have been opportunists.
There wasn’t just one kind of Zionist. An early supporter of Zionism, for example, was George Eliot. The name rings no bells, though in my dream at least, a sizeable proportion of the Jew-haters are reading English literature at university. Not the kind of English literature I studied. Not Keats and negative capability. More Edward Said and settler-colonialism.
“She wrote Middlemarch and Daniel Deronda,” I explain. The “she” throws them. Didn’t I say George Eliot? The possibility that this early proponent of Zionism might have been trans causes a brief perplexity. It would be a good idea for me to wake up at this moment. Count their confusion a victory. But my obsession forces me to continue throwing words and ideas into the unresponsive blackness.
I move on to genocide. The genocide, they invariably call it. The definite article is not accidental. We are talking about a genocide like no other. “This is not just genocide, this is IDF genocide.”
Seldom can that little word “the” have been sent on so deadly an errand. Not only does its definiteness brook no question as to the genocide’s existence, it reduces in significance and atrocity, indeed it replaces, any other genocide we might have heard about. Out you go, Jews. We have new, more deserving victims.
I set the grammar to one side and contest the definition. I know about genocides. They were once another of my obsessions. Most Jews of my acquaintance are the same. We know that a genocide is not determined by the numbers of people killed in a cruel war.
Until you understand the history and moral atmospherics of genocide, until you’ve been hounded out of every country, herded on to death trains, seen your civilisation defamed, your every thought ground to nothing, the very principle of your existence eradicated, wiped forever (had the genocide succeeded) from the slate of history – and I would not wish that experience upon a single Palestinian – until then, you who march and demonstrate against Israel have no business with the word.
Could there be such a phenomenon as Shoah-envy? Could it be that Jews are begrudged the Holocaust for the pity it earned them? Why else this attempt to render them unworthy of their history? Why else want it expunged? And now consider this: even as you march to denounce the genocide, you are wishing that very eventuality upon the Jews. I have seen posters calling on someone to finish the job. Not just from the river to the sea, but wherever and whenever Jews have been respected, you want them gone.
Even in the darkness I see the gleams of hatred in your eyes. You are excited. A flame has been lit and you want to ensure it goes on burning. I saw you pull the posters of hostages from walls and lampposts, laughing as you did so. Out you go, Jews. There’s a lesson here: speak not loosely of genocide lest it recognise itself in your words and deeds.
As things stand, a number of London universities are planning a march to commemorate Oct 7, 2023. Think of that – a festive parade to celebrate the killing of Jews. It might not go ahead as grandly as its organisers hope, but the much-abused right-to-protest argument will surely prevail against jittery authorities. Quite what the students will be protesting is hard to grasp, given that they’ve been delighting openly and freely in the bloodbath since the hour it happened.
But no one wants to question a marcher unless he marches with his face covered and goes down the street shouting in a manner which Angela Rayner has just observed she finds “intimidating” and would like not to be allowed. So just when exactly, I wonder, can a march be deemed intimidating. When the marchers cover their faces with balaclavas. And when isn’t a march intimidating? When it intimidates me.
Only a few months after Keir Starmer stepped down, the Labour Party is already a different beast. In the rush to apologise to party members for not listening to them earlier, Ed Miliband leads the pack. Sorry about Gaza, he says; we should have listened. Ask “Listen to whom exactly?” and the answer would seem to be, those calling for a ceasefire even before Hamas had finished dragging the last hostages over the border and those who want not to mention Hamas at all.
With regard to his own failure to hear these voices, Mr Miliband drips contrition. He has even brushed up on the vocabulary beloved of those he wants to please. Ethnic cleansing – tick. Settler terrorism – tick. Apartheid – tick. Illegal occupation – tick, tick, tick.
Quite how a country founded on such illegality was able to offer his traumatised grandmother the shelter and sanctuary he often talks about, he doesn’t say. But when he starts to enter my dreams I will remind him of what Israel has existed against all the odds to do. You say you are grateful, Foreign Secretary, but gratitude should be more than a word. You should feel it in that part of yourself you describe as “proudly Jewish”.
No one asks you to lie, prevaricate or whitewash. I agree that a true friend of Israel will not flinch from being critical. But the word critical has many meanings, and a true friend of Israel will not embrace the propaganda of its enemies. Seek the approval of the baying mob if you must, Mr Miliband – that’s a question for your conscience – but don’t mistake its words for “just criticism”.
Truth is a precious commodity. You won’t find it paying lickspittle to the Left of your party, many of whom, had they been around, would have smothered in its cradle the Israel that helped your grandmother. You allude to the Hamas massacre but can only scrape together a perfunctory sentence about it.
You stand emphatically, you say with weak emphasis, against those who seek Israel’s destruction, but you call Israel’s response to that barbaric massacre “a stain on the conscience of the world”. And the precipitating massacre itself? Do you not consider such barbarity a stain on the conscience of those who encouraged and then applauded it?
But if you can’t bring yourself to go that far, for fear of incurring the wrath of backbenchers who don’t accept the concept of a terrorist, tell me how exactly you intend to help keep Israel safe for future grandmothers fleeing Jew-hatred. Or do you think Hamas will take care of them?
I bat the questions into the night but there are no answers. Somewhere in the darkness is a gooey-eyed, self-pronouncing proud Jew who can’t find a good word for the Jewish state and so must borrow all the bad ones from Jew-haters of every stripe, from armed jihadis to elderly suburban anti-Semites who can’t wait to be arrested for sitting on the grass in support of Palestine Action.
What say you, Mr Miliband? While we’re talking stains on consciences, how clean is yours? I wait, but only a little white ball comes back.
I am obsessed with the ignorance of the Jew-haters
Anti-Semitism finds its fiercest home on university campuses, where students might be expected to understand history

Joseph Molloy used the "sophisticated" scam to evade £5,900 in fares from Southeastern
A former HSBC executive has been banned from working in financial services after evading thousands of pounds in train fares.
Listen to this article
Joseph Molloy, 53, has been prohibited by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) from performing any regulated activity.
He was convicted of the train fare fraud earlier this year.
The FCA said his conviction demonstrates that he ‘lacks honesty and integrity.’
Molloy admitted fraud by false representation in February after using a ticketing scam known as "doughnutting" to reduce the cost of his commute between Orpington and Canary Wharf.
It involves buying tickets for the start and finish of a journey but avoiding payment for a section in the middle.
He used the tactic at least 740 times between October 2023 and September 2024, saving nearly £6,000.
Molloy received a 10-month prison sentence suspended for 18 months. He was also ordered to complete 80 hours of unpaid work, pay £5,000 compensation and was banned from using Southeastern services for a year.

articles.title: Ukraine’s New FP-9 Ballistic Missile With Moscow in Range to Be Ready This Fall, Zelenskyy Says - UNITED24 Media
articles.summary: Ukraine’s New FP-9 Ballistic Missile With Moscow in Range to Be Ready This Fall, Zelenskyy Says  UNITED24 MediaZelenskyy: FP-9 ballistic missile capable of reaching Moscow will be ready this autumn  Українська правдаUkraine war briefing: Zelenskyy says new ballistic missile used in combat  The GuardianUkraine Fires Hard-to-Stop Ballistic Missile for First Time  WSJUkraine Reports First Combat Use of Its Own Ballistic Missile  The New York Times
articles.full_text:
Ukraine expects its domestically developed FP-9 ballistic missile, a longer-range weapon that its manufacturer says is capable of reaching Moscow, to be ready this fall, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
According to Reuters on October 3, Zelenskyy said he had personally contacted Ukrainian defense company Fire Point and urged the manufacturer to accelerate work on the FP-9 following the first combat deployment of Ukraine’s shorter-range FP-7 ballistic missile.
“I said to them, where is my FP-9?” Zelenskyy told Reuters. “We need the FP-9. And the FP-9 will be (ready) this autumn, I’m sure.”
The FP-9 is being developed as a significantly longer-range ballistic system than the FP-7. Fire Point has previously said the missile would have sufficient range to reach Moscow from Ukrainian territory.
The missile has a stated range of up to 855 kilometers and is designed to carry a warhead weighing up to 800 kilograms. The ground-launched system is intended to give Ukraine a domestically produced capability for striking targets deep behind Russian lines.
Zelenskyy’s comments came days after Ukraine announced the first combat use of the domestically produced FP-7 tactical ballistic missile. Reuters reported that the FP-7 has a range of approximately 250 kilometers.
The deployment marked another step in Ukraine’s effort to expand its domestic long-range strike capabilities as Kyiv seeks to reduce its dependence on foreign-supplied missile systems.
In the same interview, Zelenskyy told Reuters that Ukraine plans to intensify strikes against Russian oil refineries in response to Moscow’s expanding attacks against Ukrainian energy, transport, and other infrastructure. He said Kyiv would focus on facilities supporting Russia’s war effort rather than indiscriminately targeting civilian infrastructure.
“We have to respond in any way (we can). With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refiners etc: what gives money to them for this war,” Zelenskyy said. “But we will not respond, of course, just like them, on any civilian objects.”
Ukraine has increasingly invested in domestically developed missiles and long-range drones as restrictions, limited inventories, and dependence on foreign partners have constrained the availability of Western long-range weapons.
Earlier, Fire Point CEO and CTO Iryna Terekh said the FP-9 had entered the final stage of development and was expected to be completed by the end of fall 2026. The missile is designed for a range of about 850 kilometers, sufficient to reach Moscow from Ukrainian territory.

articles.summary: North Korea fires intermediate-range missile, claiming evasive flight and AI features  EuronewsNorth Korea launches ballistic missile after Seoul demands apology over wounded soldiers  The GuardianNorth Korea missile could put Guam in range as Kim rebuffs Trump outreach: expert  foxnews.comNorth Korea says Kim oversaw hypersonic missile drill  ReutersNorth Korea fires ballistic missile after Seoul demands apology over border mine blasts  Sky News
articles.full_text:
Japan’s military said the missile landed in waters outside its exclusive economic zone, while South Korea's military, which often accuses the North of exaggerating its capabilities, said it travelled more than 700 kilometres.
North Korea announced Saturday that it had test-fired an intermediate-range ballistic missile, claiming the weapon can manoeuvre in flight to evade missile defences in South Korea and Japan.
The launch comes as tensions between the two Koreas run high over landmine explosions along their border.
Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said her brother oversaw the test. She called the missile "strategic", a term that suggests it is meant to carry nuclear warheads. She also claimed it can alter its trajectory at low altitudes and has unspecified artificial intelligence capabilities, which she said would make it extremely hard to intercept.
Japan’s military said the missile landed in waters outside its exclusive economic zone, while the South Korean military, which often accuses North Korea of exaggerating its military capabilities, said the missile travelled more than 700 kilometres.
North Korea claims new missile capabilities
According to South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff, the North Korean missile was fired early Saturday from the eastern coastal Wonsan area. Japan's Defense Ministry later put the distance at roughly 680 kilometres.
In her statement, Kim Yo Jong pointed to the gap between the two US allies' figures as proof that they could not follow the missile in flight.
"Whenever we applied the wavelike trajectory mode to missiles, the enemy failed to track the targets from their first skip points," she said. "There is no way to avoid this attack."
The launch followed a day after she mocked Seoul's demand that Pyongyang apologise for the 21 September landmine explosions. The blasts went off about 10 metres south of the military demarcation line and wounded three South Korean soldiers.
A joint inspection by South Korea and the US-led United Nations Command concluded that North Korea had planted the mines, and the command later found that Pyongyang had breached the armistice that halted the 1950-53 Korean War.
Seoul has also asked the North to stop fortifying the border with mines and anti-tank barriers. That work has sped up since Kim Jong Un dropped the goal of reconciliation in 2024 and branded Seoul a permanent adversary.
Kim Yo Jong, who may be the second most powerful person in Pyongyang, called Seoul's demands "utterly pathetic" on Friday and rejected any North Korean responsibility for the blasts, warning of retaliation if the South fires on troops working along the border.
Pyongyang's weapons tests are piling up
The Wonsan launch is the newest in a string of recent military displays, which also include missile tests, live-fire drills and the commissioning of a new warship. Kim Jong Un is showing off his expanding nuclear programme even as Washington urges a return to diplomacy.
Wonsan also hosted the Sept. 20 test of what state media described as a hypersonic missile system. It belongs to a family of weapons built to overwhelm missile defences in South Korea and Japan, including solid-fuel intermediate-range missiles first revealed in 2024.
South Korea's military said it had raised its surveillance level for further launches and was sharing information closely with Washington and Tokyo. The US Pacific Command said the launch "does not pose an immediate threat to American personnel or territory or to our allies."
Kim has mostly turned his back on diplomacy with the US and South Korea since his nuclear talks with President Donald Trump broke down in 2019. He has shifted his focus to Moscow, sending thousands of troops and large shipments of weapons to back Vladimir Putin's war in Ukraine. After years of heavier testing, his arsenal of nuclear-capable missiles now includes long-range systems that could potentially reach the U.S. mainland and shorter-range ones that threaten South Korea and Japan.
In August, Trump scaled back a large joint exercise with South Korea, apparently hoping to restart talks.
North Korea has brushed off the overture, insisting that Washington first end its "hostile policy", a phrase Pyongyang uses to describe US-led sanctions and joint military drills with South Korea.

articles.title: Royal Mail delays cause Cumbrians to miss hospital appointments and bills - nwemail.co.uk
articles.summary: Royal Mail delays cause Cumbrians to miss hospital appointments and bills  nwemail.co.ukRoyal Mail responds as Gloucestershire area complains of 'terrible' post delays  Gloucestershire LiveRoyal Mail didn’t deliver my Father’s Day card – so I went to get it myself and they tried to charge me  The Independent'I dread coming to work': Royal Mail workers lift lid on Bridgwater mail chaos  bridgwatermercury.co.ukRoyal Mail 'Deliveries Today' update lists postc...
articles.full_text:
Lengthy delays in Royal Mail letter deliveries have caused South Cumbrians to miss key hospital appointments and bills.
We have spoken to a number of local residents, from Askam to Kendal, who told of letters arriving weeks late and in large amounts all at once.
Some even spoke of going to the sorting office themselves to pick up their post.
A Royal Mail spokesperson acknowledged short-term pressures sometimes cause delays and said they are recruiting more staff locally and investing £500m nationally over five years to improve reliability.
Kit Saunders, of Kendal, is one of many who have missed hospital appointments because her letter turned up after the appointment date.
She said: “I don’t care if Royal Mail say they are understaffed, or whatever else they claim. I want my post delivered in a timely manner, not at random, and certainly not two or three weeks late.”
The 46-year-old said she recently returned home from holiday on September 20, after leaving five days earlier, to a pile of post dated the 3rd.
This included house insurance renewal letters, bank letters and even one from her dentist about changing her dental plan.
Ms Saunders said: “This has been going on for years to some degree, but it is very clear that post is now being intentionally held and only being delivered in batches.
“Why the hospital still insist on sending letters is one thing, but Royal Mail not bothering to deliver them is quite another.”
Ms Saunders, as many others we spoke to, didn’t blame her “fantastic” local posties for the delays but said “they can only deliver what they are given to deliver”.
The complaints come weeks after a retiring postman from Millom previously said late deliveries were because posties were being told to prioritise parcels.
Royal Mail said their latest figures show 84.8 per cent of First-Class letters are delivered the next working day in the LA postcode, below the 93 per cent target set by postal regulator Ofcom.
Sarah Ross, 40, of Kendal, has two young children with additional health needs and her experience of missed appointments echoes that of Ms Saunder’s.
She said: “We have a lot of hospital appointments and whenever I am aware that one is almost due, I feel very anxious waiting to see if the letter will arrive or not.
“I have had occasions in the past year when the letter has not arrived until after the appointment date and so we have missed it altogether.”
Ms Ross said, on top of this, schools are clamping down on absences and won’t approve her son’s medical absences without a named letter as proof, meaning the lack of post has caused his attendance record to fall.
“We regularly go two weeks or more with no post, and then get a bundle through all at once, dated as far as 24 days prior to delivery,” said Ms Ross.
“It is having a huge impact on people's lives, especially financially with late fees on bills and on people's health.
“Missed appointments require rescheduling at a later date, which can be a significant amount of time due to the current waiting times within the NHS.”
Ofcom, the postal regulator, launched an investigation into Royal Mail earlier this year after it missed annual delivery targets yet again.
The company has been fined £37m since 2024 for failing to meet its targets with the latest figures showing 24.3 per cent of first-class mail failed to arrive within one working day in the year to the end of March.
The same figures published by Royal Mail showed that it managed to deliver 90.2 per cent of second-class mail within three-working-days, far short of Ofcom’s target of 98.5%.
Tanya Park, 46, of Carnforth, runs her own business and said the delays have made doing so increasingly challenging.
She said: “Luckily, most of our day-to-day business communication is now done by email, but we still receive cheques, bills and important documents through the post.
“Delays can make running a business more difficult, particularly when you don’t know whether something has actually been sent or is simply sitting somewhere waiting to be delivered.”
She said the most concerning experience with the delays wasn’t business related though.
Her husband was diagnosed with cancer last year and she said important time-sensitive appointment letters for tests and treatments arrived weeks after the letter’s date several times.
Ms Park said: “After we very nearly missed one appointment because of this, we made sure the hospital also notified us of any upcoming appointments by text.
“Thankfully, that meant we didn’t actually miss any, but we shouldn’t have to put a backup system in place because we can’t rely on an important hospital letter arriving in time.”
In April, Royal Mail faced criticism as it raised the price of a first-class stamp by 10p to £1.80, the cost of a first-class stamp has more than doubled since 2020.
Ms Park said: “No other business could expect its customers to keep paying more while providing an increasingly unreliable service.
“Something needs to change, both for the customers who depend on Royal Mail and for the postal workers who are being left to deal with the consequences.”
In response to the issues raised in the article, a Royal Mail spokesperson said: “We know how important it is that customers receive their mail when expected, particularly important items such as hospital appointments.
“Mail continues to be delivered across Kendal every day, although individual routes can occasionally be affected by short-term pressures. When this happens, our teams work to deliver any outstanding mail as quickly as possible.
“We are also recruiting for a number of roles at Kendal Delivery Office to further strengthen the local team.
They added they were also rolling out a new delivery model nationally across all 1,200 delivery offices to provide a more consistent service for customers.

articles.title: Google set to defend £1.2bn UK lawsuit over ‘excessive’ app download charges - ft.com
articles.summary: Google set to defend £1.2bn UK lawsuit over ‘excessive’ app download charges  ft.comSee more headlines and perspectives on Google News
articles.full_text:
Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
Google is preparing to defend a £1.2bn lawsuit over claims that millions of UK consumers have been overcharged for downloads on Android smartphones for more than a decade, in the latest legal challenge to the market power of Big Tech.
Barring a last-minute settlement, a seven-week trial is due to begin in London this week in a class action case against Google financed by Fortress Investment Group, backed by Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala investment arm.
About 20mn consumers could be in line to receive about £60 each on average if the antitrust claim is successful.
The case alleges Alphabet, Google’s parent company, has choked off competition and levied “excessive” charges on software downloaded from the Google Play Store for its Android operating system since 2015.
Google denies the claim that it has engaged in any anti-competitive conduct. In its legal defence, it contends that Android offers more choice than rivals while the Play Store helps protect customers from cyber security threats.
The lawsuit follows a legal breakthrough in a similar case last year against Apple, which the Competition Appeal Tribunal found had imposed unfair charges on downloads from its App Store.
Apple is challenging the judgment and the Court of Appeal is due to hear the case next year.
Google in August agreed to pay £260mn to settle a related UK case brought on behalf of thousands of software developers over commissions it imposes on Play Store downloads.
The claimants in the forthcoming trial are led by “class representative” and consumer policy specialist Liz Coll, who contends that excessive charges levied on software developers have been passed on to everyday users through higher prices.
Coll told the FT that many consumers were unaware that Google had charged commission fees as high as 30 per cent on mobile software, such as gaming, dating and music-streaming apps.
In 2023, Google lost a high-profile case brought in California by Epic Games, maker of popular video games such as Fortnite, which successfully argued that Google’s exclusive deals and revenue-sharing arrangements with smartphone makers, network operators and game developers were illegal.
The San Francisco judge ordered Google to open its Android operating system to rivals so they can create their own app marketplaces and payment systems. After a series of appeals, Google and Epic agreed to settle the case in March this year.
Also in 2023, Google paid $700mn to settle a US antitrust lawsuit brought by multiple states that alleged that it conspired to shut out rival payment systems and then overcharge customers.
Coll is calling for compensation for subscriptions and in-app purchases such as gaming add-ons, which have become an important source of revenue for tech groups.
“Of course there’s a case that it’s a drop in the ocean for the company, but I think there’s something really valid and important in people knowing that they can’t do whatever they want and that there’s recourse to some kind of redress,” Coll said. “I think you can make dents in some parts of the empire.”
The claim alleges that Google imposed barriers on rival app stores and forced mobile phone manufacturers to preinstall the Play Store on new devices.
The £1.2bn figure was the claimants’ estimate of possible damages, based in part on the tribunal’s findings in the case against Apple, Coll added.
Any compensation awarded would depend on several factors, including how much of the alleged “overcharge” the tribunal deems to have been passed on from developers to consumers.
Google says the commissions it charges have reduced over time.
In its defence of the claim filed with the tribunal, the company also noted that the vast majority of Play Store apps were free and only about 3 per cent of the largest app developers paid any fee.
It argued that a proliferation of unverified new app stores and payment methods on Android could harm customers by increasing scams and fraud.
“Android gives people more choice than any other mobile platform in deciding which apps and app stores they use, with Play offering some of the lowest fees in the market,” Google said. “This lawsuit ignores that choice as well as the competitive market in which we operate, and we will defend our services vigorously.”

Israeli embassies in the United States and the United Kingdom are promoting a copycat NAZA, nearly a month after the release of the original that focuses on testimony of Israelis killing Palestinians in Gaza.
In posts on X, the embassies said that "Naza: The Real Story" is "setting the record straight" and claims to offer a firsthand account from senior Israeli military commanders and intelligence officers directly involved in Israel's genocidal war on Gaza.
It said the film uses combat footage, declassified materials, captured intelligence and firsthand testimony to give context on "how the war was fought and the challenges Israeli forces faced".
The film's website names the provider as Three Musketeers Production, "a company in formation", and says a registered address and registration number will be published once the company is registered. It says the directors are deliberately not named "for their safety".
Claimed to have been filmed on the rooftops of Tel Aviv, the 49-minute documentary is available in 17 languages on its official website.
"Rooftop interviews with senior IDF [Israeli army] commanders: Hamas fighters in civilian clothes, hostages held in homes, aid and Hamas. For people about to watch this film, not a NASA picture," reads a blog entry about the film.
The website lists a release date of 20 September 2026 and says the film will also be shown in theatres.
Blog posts on the film's website, dated 18-26 September, summarise interviews it says are included in the documentary.
"One interview covers Gaza from north to south. No personal names appear on this page, and the directors are unnamed for security reasons," the website notes.
"This page summarises what the interviewee says. It reports his account and the IDF rules he describes. It does not verify them independently."
'Hang the traitors'
Directed by Israeli journalists Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, NAZA: A Window into Systems of Mass Killing has riled the Israeli government and far-right elements of Israeli society since its premiere and Special Jury Prize win at the Venice International Film Festival last month.
The 25-minute standing ovation for the film set a new record for any movie at a major festival, surpassing the near 24 minutes by The Voice of Hind Rajab at last year's Venice festival.
NAZA examines the AI-powered systems used in Israel's war on Gaza and allegations that high numbers of Palestinian civilian deaths were factored into military targeting decisions.
The documentary features interviews with 24 Israeli military and intelligence insiders, whose identities remained anonymous.
Israeli politicians, journalists and members of the public have attacked Szor and Abraham, accusing them of treason and calling for their citizenship to be revoked.
Last month, Culture Minister Miki Zohar called the film "despicable" and said he would "act immediately to revoke the Israeli citizenship of these despicable creators on the grounds of treason against the state".
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu joined Zohar in attacking the filmmakers, saying he would introduce two bills targeting those who "defame" the Israeli military.
Netanyahu said the first bill "would revoke the citizenship of anyone who defames soldiers", while the second would increase "twentyfold the amount in damages for which they can be sued for defamation".
"They have no place among us," Netanyahu said of those who "defame" the Israeli army.
The Israeli military's Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir has ordered legal action against Szor and Abraham with the help of the Shin Bet, according to Israeli media.
Dozens of far-right Israelis gathered outside Szor's family home on 16 September, demanding she be hanged.
The Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported that several of the protesters demanded the "death penalty for traitors".
One demonstrator said that when Szor and Abraham return to Israel, "they should be tried and go to the gallows, and the family should be expelled and the house sealed".
Many social media users dismissed the documentary as "propaganda" and an attempt to "bury the real film".
An X account named Britain United wrote: "Pathetic, that actual Naza documentary must be really exposing for you to try to SEO bury the real film online by using the same title."
"You can try and spin the Israeli slaughter of the residents of Gaza all you want, but it won't work," X user Joe said.

articles.title: Fed and ECB Dial Back Near-Term Hike Urgency After Soft US Jobs, French Market Strain - Briefs Finance
articles.summary: Fed and ECB Dial Back Near-Term Hike Urgency After Soft US Jobs, French Market Strain  Briefs Finance
articles.full_text:
Central banks ease up on near-term moves
Jittery markets and softer data have taken some air out of hawkish bets. After both lifted benchmark rates in September, the Fed and ECB will publish their meeting records this week - the Fed on Wednesday, the ECB on Thursday - and the vibe inside the rooms will matter.
Two influential Fed officials have already signaled there is little urgency. Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson and New York Fed President John Williams, in appearances two days apart, indicated they did not see a need to hurry. Investors trimmed rate-hike expectations accordingly. The Fed next meets Oct. 27-28, just ahead of a hotly contested midterm election.
In Europe, investors will comb the ECB's Sept. 9-10 account for timing clues. Bond stress has gone global, with France hit hard as its fractured parliament stirs concern over the budget and deficit.
Data and markets nudge policymakers toward patience
US growth has been sturdy enough to keep the job market on its feet, letting the Fed home in on inflation. September minutes could show many policymakers were deeply concerned about underlying price trends and expected to raise rates at least once more before year end.
But the latest numbers argue for waiting. Friday's report showed job creation missed forecasts and wage growth was lackluster, reinforcing the idea the labor market is not feeding current inflation pressures. Government updates to the Fed's favored inflation gauge earlier in the week showed this year's price increases came in milder than initially estimated.
Bloomberg Economics put it this way: "The hurdle for an October rate hike is now high. Even if the minutes remind markets how hawkish officials were in September, subsequent data have strengthened the case for patience. Sticky services inflation could keep open the option of a December hike - but the Fed will probably need clearer evidence that price pressures have re-emerged before tightening again." - Anna Wong, Andrew Sacher and Eliza Winger.
Across the Atlantic, September euro-area inflation quickened beyond forecasts, largely due to war-related energy costs. Even so, investors see very slim chances of an October ECB hike.
Central bank minutes tell you more about the next rate move than any forecast will. Market Briefs reads them so you do not have to, free every weekday.
A crowded global calendar: India's decision, ECB watchers, Canada data
Plenty else is on deck. About a dozen central banks will decide policy this week, and markets anticipate increases in India, Kenya and Peru.
- Asia: The Reserve Bank of India meets Wednesday, and economists expect a repurchase-rate hike to 5.5%, putting India alongside peers in Japan, Australia and the US that have tightened. Australia's Westpac consumer sentiment on Monday will likely reflect last week's rate increase. Japan will release August wage figures on Tuesday, with focus on whether inflation-adjusted earnings notch an eighth consecutive monthly gain. September inflation prints are due from Taiwan, Thailand and the Philippines, and each is expected to rise. Several countries will release foreign reserves, with South Korea, Taiwan and China watched for signs their strong trade surpluses are showing up in the totals; India and Thailand also report. China's central bank is due to announce September lending late in the week or early next week after August's slump.
- Europe, Middle East and Africa: France's fiscal worries keep the spotlight on the ECB.
Scheduled appearances include Chief Economist Philip Lane, Austria's Martin Kocher and Belgium's Pierre Wunsch, and Thursday's September account will be closely parsed.
Maneuvering for future ECB roles is intensifying: Pablo Hernandez de Cos, the Bank for International Settlements chief, and Klaas Knot, the former Dutch central bank governor - both seen as rivals to succeed President Christine Lagarde - will share a stage on Monday.
According to people familiar, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz plans to hold meetings with both candidates, including Knot, over the next few days.
Euro-zone finance ministers gather in Luxembourg on Thursday and may open discussions on who should replace Executive Board member Isabel Schnabel, with France's bond turmoil as the backdrop.
Industry data will draw attention too: beginning Tuesday, Germany will release, on back-to-back days, figures on factory orders, industrial output and exports, while France, Spain and Italy report production data throughout the week.
The region's industrial strains will loom as EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic makes a trip to Beijing later in the week.
In the UK, five Bank of England officials speak, including Governor Andrew Bailey on Thursday.
Sweden's inflation print arrives Thursday after the Riksbank's tilt toward a likely hike, and Norway - which raised rates last month - reports prices Friday.
In South Africa, Reserve Bank Governor Lesetja Kganyago speaks Tuesday at the Monetary Policy Review release.

- North America: In Canada, jobless and trade data will shed light on how its tariff confrontation with the US is playing out.
- EMEA rate decisions: Iceland will decide rates on Wednesday, coming off a pickup in inflation to a two-year high, after implementing 75 basis points of increases so far this year. Poland is likely to hold the same day. Kenya may hike for the first time since 2024 as inflation edges toward its 7.5% ceiling. On Thursday, Tanzania is likely to leave rates unchanged as inflation remains contained. Romania's central bank is seen keeping the policy rate at 6.5% amid ongoing inflation risks, and Serbia could prolong its record-length pause in tightening with pivotal general elections on the horizon.
- Latin America: On Monday, Colombia's central bank releases the record of its surprise Sept. 30 quarter-point hike to 12.25%. The split decision reflects tight monetary conditions starting to bend but not yet reversing 2026's jump in consumer prices. September inflation may validate the move, with early consensus pointing to another uptick from 6.24%, still more than twice target. Mexico will publish minutes from its September meeting and fresh inflation data. Banxico held at 6.5% for a third straight decision and shifted to data-dependent guidance; September CPI likely accelerated again. Peru and Uruguay both face tough calls this week. In Peru, inflation pushed further beyond target in September, potentially straining policymakers' resolve following a year of holding at 4.25%. Uruguay has maintained its benchmark at 5.75% since a 75 basis-point reduction.
What this means for your portfolio
The mood has shifted from sprint to stroll. If officials take more time to weigh cooler US labor data and Europe's bond jitters, the near-term path for borrowing costs could be gentler even with a possible year-end Fed move still on the table. With minutes, inflation prints and rate calls dropping worldwide, expect the rate narrative and volatility to move fast. Keep an eye on how those signals filter into the parts of your life that feel rate changes first, like credit costs and cash yields.

Defence secretary Wes Streeting has said that Donald Trump is “absolutely right” to demand the UK increase military spending significantly.
Speaking after a summit of Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF) defence ministers in Keflavik, Mr Streeting aligned his pleas with US demands for Nato allies to shoulder a larger financial burden.
“We want to be deterring Russia, and we want to make sure that if deterrence fails, we’re ready to defeat our enemies,” Mr Streeting said. “Nato-first is our policy, but also it’s why I’ve been really keen to make clear... that president Trump and his administration have been absolutely right to demand more of the UK, more of Europe.”
The intervention comes as ministers navigate domestic fiscal pressures ahead of the Budget, exposing a rift among Labour MPs over balancing military expansion against welfare spending.
Although chancellor John Healey plans to fund the Defence Investment Plan (DIP) in the immediate Budget, however a definitive blueprint to reach the 3 per cent spending rate by 2030 has been deferred to the 2027 spending review.
Mr Streeting maintained the Ministry of Defence would receive a “more than sympathetic hearing” from the Treasury, stressing the need for internal procurement reform to demonstrate value to taxpayers.
“We can’t be complacent and just assume that we can send John Healey’s resignation in as our spending review submission,” Mr Streeting noted, referencing Healey’s previous resignation over defence funding under the Starmer administration.
The push for expanded budgets faces pushback from backbench Labour MPs and prime minister Andy Burnham has previously cautioned that national security “cannot come at the expense of social security”.
Addressing military leaders at a conference last month, Mr Streeting quoted former defence secretary Denis Healey’s 1969 warning that cutting defence until security is imperilled leaves a nation with “no houses, no hospitals, no schools – we have a heap of cinders.”
“I’m happy to sing The Red Flag but this Labour government won’t wave the white flag,” Mr Streeting said, adding that military investment serves to reindustrialise Britain.
The comments coincide with heightened concerns surrounding domestic counter-terror activity. Police arrested a 25-year-old British-Iranian national over a suspected ‘foiled’ plot near RAF Fairford earlier this week, while two small-boat migrants face trial in Manchester over an alleged plot targeting the Jewish community.
Calling Tehran a “malevolent force,” Mr Streeting confirmed the government is assessing responses, including further sanctions.
On Russian posturing in the High North and Baltic regions, Mr Streeting said: “Russia is increasingly engaged in what can only be described as acts of state-sponsored terrorism,” rejecting terms like “hybrid threat.”
Separately, Nato secretary-general Mark Rutte warned during a UK visit that European democracies face severe exposure without increased outlay, noting European allies required a “shot of adrenaline” from President Trump.
To address budget shortfalls including a £4.7 billion gap in the MoD’s £15 billion investment plan, British officials met Canadian prime minister Mark Carney in Liverpool to evaluate the Canadian-led Defence, Security and Resilience Bank.
The initiative seeks to leverage government-underwritten private capital to scale defence technology – opening up an opportunity to bolster defence without directly adding to national debt.

The International Energy Agency said Saturday that member countries had so far released 325 million barrels of oil and oil-derivative products from strategic reserves, from the 400 million barrels promised in March.

articles.title: Explainer: Why Some Indian Exporters Have To Pay Europe For Carbon Emissions In India - ETV Bharat
articles.summary: Explainer: Why Some Indian Exporters Have To Pay Europe For Carbon Emissions In India  ETV Bharat
articles.full_text:
The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism puts a carbon cost on imports, calculated per tonne per product.
New Delhi: India and the European Union committed to increasing trade by concluding negotiations on the long-pending Free Trade Agreement, labelled the "mother of all deals," early this year.
But as the two-decade-long negotiations drew to a close, a wrinkle emerged in the form of the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which sets a cost on products that release a large amount of greenhouse gases, such as carbon dioxide, during manufacturing.
The CBAM came into full force on January 1, raising the possibility of higher export costs and potential diversification away from the EU market for carbon-intensive exports. Officials on both sides have continued discussions on the CBAM, ranging from how India's own carbon pricing policy will be factored into the carbon price to how emissions will be calculated.
So as the two countries look to deepen trade, will CBAM prove to be a drag on carbon-intensive Indian exports like steel to the EU?
Why are companies paying for emissions in India in the EU?
The EU has the world’s biggest emissions trading market in its Emissions Trading System, which accounts for three-quarters of international carbon trading.
Within this, the CBAM is a mechanism that puts a carbon cost on imports, calculated per tonne per product.
CBAM is applied to carbon-intensive products such as iron, steel, aluminium, cement, fertilisers, hydrogen, and electricity imported into the EU.
On steel, for instance, the rate will be calculated according to the carbon intensity of the specific steel production multiplied by the EU Emissions Trading System which is around €70–€80 per tonne of carbon dioxide (CO₂) with any free allocations and carbon price paid domestically also factored into the final Carbon rate.
The EU implemented the definitive CBAM regime from January 1 this year to put non-EU manufacturers on par with domestic ones who pay carbon rates. But importers will only have to start submitting the CBAM certificates next year, with annual declarations by September.
In order to implement CBAM, manufacturers first calculate the carbon emitted per tonne of production and then report the emissions. Importers are required to buy CBAM certificates to cover those emissions.
Put simply, an Indian steel producer, exporting to the EU, will provide verified emissions data or carbon emitted per tonne of production to the EU importer who would then calculate the carbon rate and buy CBAM certificates for the corresponding carbon rates. The importer will then submit the certificate as payment.
Though CBAM costs are paid by the importers, the cost is passed down to non-EU exporters or manufacturers in the form of lower prices or reduced margins for importers. If the EU finds incorrect emission details have been submitted, the fine includes €100 per tonne of Co2 equivalent.
A key aim of the CBAM for the EU is to prevent carbon leakage or prevent companies from moving production overseas to countries with less stringent climate rules.
Indian exporters to feel the carbon pinch
While India’s CBAM-exposed exports to the EU account for only 0.2 per cent of its GDP, the iron and steel sector constitutes 90 per cent of these exports, making the sector "particularly vulnerable", according to a report by think tank Centre for Social and Economic Progress (CSEP). India exports around $75.85 billion worth of goods to the EU with 10 per cent of this attracting CBAM for now.
According to CSEP, Indian steel exports are vulnerable due to the industry’s relatively higher carbon footprint compared to their European counterparts. For instance, India averages roughly 2.3 to 2.5 tonnes of CO₂ per tonne of crude steel, higher than the EU benchmark of 1.37 and world average benchmark of 1.92.
Studies and analysts believe that, as a result of the CBAM smaller manufacturers who operate on smaller margins may not be able to pay the cost of decarbonising their business. Analysts also believe that exporters might look for alternative markets that do not have such a carbon pricing policy.
According to an estimate by the Global Trade Research, CBAM will force Indian steel and aluminium exporters to slash prices by 15 to 22 per cent to stay competitive.
Why is CBAM linked to climate justice?
Beyond the trade aspect, there is a larger issue concerning CBAM. International treaties have recognised that developed countries have a greater responsibility towards climate change as they contributed the most and have more resources to adopt clean technologies and create solutions.
The criticism is that revenue under CBAM moves away from developing nations and emerging economies, which require climate funds, into the EU, which is imposing its environmental standards on countries that have different levels of development.
So the question is whether developed nations, that share a larger burden of historical emissions and pollution, should face the CBAM. India has criticised the CBAM as arbitrary and a protectionist non-tariff trade barrier that violates core multilateral trade rules at the World Trade Organisation (WTO).
While India is engaged in CBAM discussions with the EU, it is closely tracking proceedings brought by Russia at the WTO against the CBAM alleging it is a trade barrier and an export subsidy under the EU emissions trading system. The WTO's dispute settlement body in September agreed to Russia's request for a panel to examine the CBAM in a test for the EU.
How are exporters being protected?
While the EU is not providing any CBAM waivers, it has provided a tariff-rate quota of 1.9 million tonnes (MT) annually, meaning the limit on how much steel a particular country can export to the EU without paying extra taxes.
Within India, the government has started creating awareness among exporters, particularly small and medium-sized firms, and is also looking at developing a mechanism for measuring the embedded emissions and providing financial assistance for smaller players under the Export Promotion Mission
Most importantly India is also rolling out its own Carbon Credit Trading Scheme to mitigate overseas tax liabilities.
Still, exporters feel much more needs to be done and are also pushing for the domestic Carbon Credit Trading Scheme to be formally recognised by the EU, which remains under discussion between the two sides.
How India handles CBAM will be critical, as carbon trading is increasingly adopted by other countries and Indian exports will have to increasingly adopt clean technologies to make exports more competitive.

articles.title: Poland brings civilians back into European war plans - Tomorrow's Affairs
articles.summary: Poland brings civilians back into European war plans  Tomorrow's Affairs
articles.full_text:
In Lublin, in eastern Poland, an anti-aircraft shelter from the mid-1980s, built beneath the premises of the city’s bus company, is back in operation.
After renovation, it can accommodate 200 people and supply them with air, water and electricity for three days, independently of the public network.
One change also carries symbolic weight: the emergency exit now faces west instead of east.
When the shelter was built, Poland was part of the Soviet bloc and, according to official doctrine, the enemy was expected to come from the west. Today, the danger comes from the opposite direction.
That shelter is not a museum piece. Poland is on high alert after several incursions by Russian missiles and drones into its airspace, with residents of eastern regions receiving evacuation warnings whenever Russia attacks western Ukraine.
Last week, a regional television station interrupted a live programme for 20 minutes because its journalists had to take shelter.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk said at a cabinet meeting this week that Poland is scrambling fighter jets day and night because Russian attacks on western Ukraine, right next to the Polish border, have become a daily occurrence.
In recent years, Poland has spent tens of billions of euros on tanks, missile systems, aircraft and ammunition, and for 2026 it has allocated about 200 billion Polish zlotys for defence, approximately 51.3 billion dollars, or 4.81 per cent of GDP.
Increasingly, security funding is being directed towards the less visible challenge of keeping cities, hospitals, water systems, the power grid and millions of civilians functioning if the country comes under prolonged attack.
The scale of that task is best illustrated by the numbers. About 2,000 fully equipped shelters have space for around 300,000 people, fewer than one per cent of the population of 38 million.
Poland has also recorded more than 86,000 basements, underground garages, underground stations and other spaces that could accommodate about 23 million people, but most do not have ventilation, autonomous power supplies, water or other systems that purpose-built shelters have. Even today, many citizens do not know where to take shelter.
In recent years, European security policy has focused on increasing troop numbers, ammunition stocks, air defence and fighter jets.
The war in Ukraine has shown how heavily military capability depends on energy, transport, telecommunications and healthcare.
A power outage hampers military operations and logistics, a damaged railway slows the movement of units and equipment, a communication breakdown disrupts crisis management, and hospitals must care for civilians and soldiers simultaneously.
Poland did not have to learn that lesson only from Ukraine. In November 2025, an explosive device destroyed part of the railway from Warsaw to Lublin near the village of Mika and, on the same line, overhead contact lines were destroyed.
This is the railway used to send aid to Ukraine. The Polish authorities have accused two Ukrainian citizens of the attack, who, they claim, worked for the Russian intelligence service.
Warsaw subsequently closed the last Russian consulate in the country and deployed thousands of troops to guard critical infrastructure.
Civilian systems are not only a target in war; they are being attacked now, below the threshold that would trigger allied defences
Civilian systems, therefore, are not only a target in war; they are being attacked now, below the threshold that would trigger allied defences.
That is why Poland is now including these systems in its defence planning, and this has immediate security value.
A strike on the power grid, railways or telecommunications has the greatest effect when it causes long-term disruption, mass displacement and pressure on state institutions.
The faster the state restores basic services and organises daily life during an attack, the less benefit an adversary can expect from targeting civilian infrastructure.
Civil protection thus becomes part of deterrence. Military power remains its foundation, but the state’s ability to withstand a serious blow depends increasingly on how quickly it can restore key civilian systems.
Poland has begun to turn that problem into budgetary and legal obligations. The Act on Civil Protection and Civil Defence of December 2024 stipulates that at least 0.3 per cent of GDP must be allocated annually to these tasks.
For 2025 and 2026, a total of almost 34 billion zlotys, about 8.7 billion dollars, is planned for a system much broader than shelters alone.
The programme covers backup water and energy supplies, warning systems, communications, medical facilities, stockpiles of supplies and equipment, training for services and citizens, and the organisation of civil defence.
The Ministry of the Interior is also preparing the next programme, for the period from 2027 to 2031, with a preliminary budget of at least 105 billion zlotys, or about 27 billion dollars.
The programme still awaits final government approval, but it clearly shows the scale of the change.
Civil protection is being transformed from an occasional item into a permanent public function
Civil protection is being transformed from an occasional item related to floods, fires and industrial accidents into a permanent public function, to which a substantial share of state funds will be allocated in advance.
The distribution of that money also reveals the plan’s weakest point. For 2027, at least 23.4 billion zlotys, about 6 billion dollars, is planned, and for 2028 more than 24.7 billion, about 6.3 billion dollars.
After that, the amounts fall to 18.4 billion zlotys in 2029, about 4.7 billion dollars, then to 19 billion in 2030, about 4.9 billion dollars, and to 19.5 billion in 2031, about 5 billion dollars.
Funding is thus already reduced by about a quarter within the government’s own plan, before the legal standard of protection is even approximately achieved.
The figures themselves should not be read literally. The statutory 0.3 per cent of GDP partially overlaps with broader defence spending, so that amount cannot simply be added to the military budget and presented as entirely new expenditure.
Most of the implementation will fall on local authorities and operators who manage cities on a daily basis.
Their tasks will include determining which facilities can be used as shelters, providing backup power for waterworks and hospitals, defining evacuation routes and the movement of military columns, and agreeing what should be repaired first if communications or the transport network are damaged. Central government can provide funding and set standards, but actual readiness will depend on what is done on the ground.
The standard is set high. The law requires cities to provide shelter for at least half of the people who may find themselves in their territory at the time of danger, and part of that capacity must be in facilities with a higher level of protection.
From 2026, the obligation to provide protected space will also apply to new public and multi-family residential buildings, thus returning shelters to urban planning after several decades.
Between the current figure of fewer than one per cent of places in actual shelters and the legal target lies a multi-year programme of construction and adaptation of existing buildings. Such infrastructure cannot be created within a single budget year.
At the end of 2025 and the beginning of 2026, almost 17 million copies of a safety manual were delivered to every Polish household, with instructions for power failures, evacuation, air raids, cyber incidents and other crisis situations. More important than the document itself is the state’s changed attitude towards the population.
Citizens are once again treated as part of the civil defence system, with predefined procedures, a practice that disappeared in much of Europe after the Cold War. T
he new programme includes practical workshops for citizens and further development of the Civil Defence Corps, because a manual in the letterbox is not yet a practised response.
The Polish programme is gaining wider importance due to changes within NATO. After the 2025 Hague summit, members will be able to count up to 1.5 per cent of GDP towards a broader security investment category that includes infrastructure, resilience and civil preparedness.
On 15 September, the Alliance announced for the first time the new requirements for member states’ resilience.
Allies are required to have plans for the continuity of government; energy, food and water supplies; health; communications and transport operations; and for the ability of civilian infrastructure to support military operations.
It is particularly important that states determine in advance how they will share limited resources between the population, their own armed forces and allied units that would arrive as reinforcements.
That framework is reshaping the political economy of European defence. Much future security spending will flow through the budgets of cities, energy companies, hospitals, telecoms operators, railways and the construction sector.
Poland is the most interesting case here because it already has a large civil protection programme
Private owners of key infrastructure will have to plan their operations for severe crisis conditions, and governments will have to decide who pays for backup systems and supplies that may not be needed for years under normal circumstances.
The same framework also creates scope for accounting tricks. Under NATO rules, resilience and civil defence expenditure is recognised if it is based on national resilience planning or required to carry out allied plans.

articles.title: France is the Biggest Loser in the Global Rates Reset - The Overshoot
articles.summary: France is the Biggest Loser in the Global Rates Reset  The Overshoot
articles.full_text:
Borrowing costs are up everywhere. And France—thanks to its dysfunctional domestic conditions and its membership of the euro area—is getting hit the hardest.
In the years immediately before the pandemic, long-term yields on government debts in Japan and “core” Europe were roughly zero or negative before inflation, about 1% in the U.K., ~1.5% in Czechia, about 2% in Australia, Canada, the U.S., and Korea, and about 3% in Poland. As of this writing, longer-term yields are now about 3% in Japan, ~3.5% in Germany and Sweden, 4% in Canada and Spain, close to 5% in France and Korea, and a bit over 5% in Australia, the U.S., U.K., Czechia, and Poland. As far as I can tell, the only rich countries that have largely missed out on the yield reset have been Switzerland, Singapore, Taiwan, and Greece (sort of), albeit for very different reasons. In general, long-term yields in the rich countries are about 2-3 percentage points higher than they were on average in 2017-2019.
Whether this is a problem depends on where you are. A simple average across rich countries shows that the most recent 12-month nominal income growth rates are also 2pp faster than the 2017Q1-2019Q4 annualized average. But that average conceals considerable variation across countries. For many places, such as the U.S., Canada, Japan, Portugal, and Spain, there has been a one-for-one link between the uptick in yields and the change in growth rates. In a few cases, such as Taiwan, Korea, and Greece, yields have gone up by much less than one might have guessed based on how much growth has accelerated. It may not last, but the Taiwanese economy is currently growing by about 20% a year in local currency terms while the Korean economy is growing at 40% (!) thanks to soaring export earnings.
On the opposite extreme is France.
Yields on French government bonds (OATs) now exceed the yields on their Spanish, Italian (BTPs), Greek (GGBs), and Portuguese equivalents. For veterans of the euro crisis, this is a remarkable turn of events. As recently as 2024, yields on 10-year BTPs were about 1.1 percentage points higher than on 10-year OATs. But as of this writing, 10-year OATs now yield about 0.2pp more than the equivalent BTPs. The resulting 1.3pp shift in the spread has occurred in almost a straight line. While some of that move was a function of improving conditions in Italy in 2024, it mostly reflects problems in France, especially over the past few months. For example, the spread between Belgian and Italian yields has been essentially unchanged over the past year.
The problem for France is that its bond yields are surging even as its nominal income growth has slowed relative to the 2017-2019 pace, to the point that, almost uniquely among rich countries, borrowing costs there now substantially exceed growth rates. In fact, the spread between French sovereign borrowing costs and French growth rates is now the most unfavorable anywhere in the rich world.1 The French economy was not quite growing by 2% a year in euro terms as of 2026Q2, which was even worse than the anemic 3% yearly average nominal growth rate recorded in 2017Q1-2019Q4. As of 2026Q2, France’s cost of borrowing was therefore about 2pp higher than its income growth rate. (At current yields, the penalty is more like 3pp.) By contrast, Spanish and Greek bond yields are still about 2pp lower than their income growth rates.

articles.summary: The collapse of the political center – a view from the EU  Workers World
